docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Logging plays an important role in working with this model. It's how you watch a program execute instruction by instruction (see Getting Started), confirm a timing change actually took effect (see Performance Modeling), or work out why a test is failing without single-stepping a debugger. This page covers how logging is actually put together across both models, how to narrow it down to just the part of a run you care about, and how to explore the resulting trace in the bundled log viewer.

docs.title: The current scheme
docs.text:
SparcCore owns a CoreLogger (SparcCore::logger). There is one per core instance, not per driver. Both cpp_model and sitar_model drive the same SparcCore, so both produce the identical trace format from it, one tab-separated row per architectural event (fetch, trap, memory access) with the entire current-window state. This is viewable the same way in the log viewer, regardless of which model produced it. See "The log viewer" below and model/cpp_common_code/CoreLogger.h.

A driver uses CoreLogger one of two ways.

  • do_print=true (cpp_model/src/sparc_sim.cpp) CoreLogger writes each row directly to a given ostream itself.
  • do_print=false (sitar_model) Each log_*() call just returns the formatted row. The caller (SparcThread.sitar) forwards it into Sitar's own log<< mechanism instead of writing it directly.

That second path is where Sitar's own per-module logging comes in. Every Sitar module or procedure owns a sitar::logger, unrelated to CoreLogger. This is Sitar's own class, see Sitar's Logging documentation for the full mechanism. It can be pointed at:

  • A common stream Sitar's own default. setHierarchicalOstream(TOP, stream) (see sparc_sim.cpp) points every module or procedure's logger at the same ostream, so everything ends up interleaved together in one place.
  • A per-module stream Points just one procedure's .log at its own dedicated ostream. This is what sparc_sim.cpp does for sparcThread specifically. sparcThread.log.setOstream(&sparcTraceFile), plus useDefaultPrefix=false and setPrefix("") to drop Sitar's own (time)hierarchicalId: prefix, gives sparcThread's own trace: pure CoreLogger rows, nothing else, a clean file completely separate from mainMemory and the VirtualMainMemoryInterface instances' own messages (sitar.log). See model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/README.md.

Both models name that trace file after the hex file's own basename, with the trailing .hex replaced by .log (test_simple_ADD.hex produces test_simple_ADD.log, written into the current directory). Running a different test right after doesn't clobber the previous one's trace, the way a single fixed filename would.

docs.title: Compile-time on/off
docs.text:
Two macros are tied to the same --logging flag. Every configuration's cpp_model/build.sh and sitar_model/build.sh both expose it (the latter forwarding to the shared build_scripts/build_sitar_model.py). --logging passes --cflags=-DSPARC_LOGGING_ENABLED through to sitar compile alongside Sitar's own --logging, so one flag controls both.

  • SPARC_LOGGING_ENABLED Gates CoreLogger. Without it (the default), every log_*() method compiles down to a trivial return ""; stub. None of the state-collection or formatting code exists in the binary at all, not just skipped at runtime. See CoreLogger.h's file comment.
  • SITAR_ENABLE_LOGGING Gates Sitar's own sitar::logger class the same way (see sitar_logger.h in the separate sitar repo).

This is why logging is a rebuild, not a runtime flag. Formatting the entire current-window state (~50 fields) on every single instruction is real, non-negligible cost, and a --no-logging build pays literally none of it.

docs.title: Selective on/off at runtime
docs.text:
Even within a --logging build, you don't have to log everything. Sitar's sitar::logger has runtime turnON()/turnOFF()/isON() methods, checked on every log<< call. They're cheap to toggle as often as you like (see Sitar's own Logging documentation, linked above, for the full mechanism).

A commented-out example of this lives in Core.sitar: a fourth branch in the top-level parallel block, alongside sparcThread, mainMemory, and the halt-detection monitor, that turns sparcThread.log on and off each cycle based on both simulated time and PC. Copy it out and adjust the two conditions to your own needs:

||
    do
        wait until (this_phase==0);
        $
        bool inTimeWindow = current_time.cycle() >= 1000 && current_time.cycle() < 2000;
        bool inPCRange    = sparcThread.core.reg.R_PC() >= 0x2000 && sparcThread.core.reg.R_PC() < 0x2100;
        if (inTimeWindow && inPCRange)
            sparcThread.log.turnON();
        else
            sparcThread.log.turnOFF();
        $;
        wait(1,0);
    while (1) end do;

Don't drop the wait(1,0)

It matters more than it looks. Without it, this loop never lets simulated time actually advance. wait until (cond) returns immediately once cond is already true, which it still is on the very next iteration, with nothing else in the loop to change that. So it spins at the same simulated instant forever, and hits Sitar's iteration-limit safety net almost immediately. One cycle is plenty, this only needs to re-check once per cycle.

Since this toggles sparcThread.log itself, it narrows the trace file down directly. Rows outside the window or range are simply never written, not filtered out afterward, turning a long run's trace into something small and targeted enough to load into the log viewer right away.

The condition above still has to be decided in advance and built into Core.sitar. For a condition that depends on the program's own data at runtime, a register or memory location reaching a specific value, see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB instead.

docs.title: The log viewer
docs.text:
A single, self-contained HTML file, log_viewer/viewer.html, explores a trace. It needs no build step and no server, and works entirely offline. Open it directly in any browser.

It has three independently resizable panels.

  • Disassembly The .objdump of the program under test, so you can see the actual instructions alongside their addresses.
  • Trace One row per architectural event (FETCH, EXECUTED, TRAP_RAISED, MEM_READ, and so on), color coded by event type.
  • State The full processor state at whichever row is currently selected: control fields (PC, nPC, WIM, Y, TBR), PSR flags, and all four register groups (globals, outputs, locals, inputs).

Click a row in Trace to select it and see its state there. Click a line in Disassembly to jump to the first Trace row at that address. Use the Up/Down arrow keys to step through the trace row by row, regardless of any search. The search box (field=value, for example PC=0x1c or l4=0x3434) filters to matching rows, prev/next step through them.

Try the log viewer here, preloaded with a small sample trace (from the bundled test_simple_ADD example) so you can explore it right away, no build required.

To view a trace of your own, open log_viewer/viewer.html from your own clone instead, and use its Load trace/Load objdump buttons (top right) to pick a trace file you produced yourself (see "Compile-time on/off" above) and its matching .objdump. See log_viewer/README.md for the full reference, including how to serve it locally so a fresh trace auto-loads from a URL, the same way the embedded copy above does.

docs.title: Model Components
docs.text: This section describes the main components in the model, such as the SparcCore, Mmu, Memory, Caches, Devices, the system bus, and the APARA engine, in detail. For a listing of each component's model see Model Components Reference.

docs.title: SparcCore
docs.text:
SparcCore is a pure C++ class implementing SPARC V8 instruction semantics: decode dispatch, ALU/FPU operations (including quad-precision, via libquadmath), trap logic, and the full register file (windowed integer registers, f0-f31, and all state registers). It has no notion of cycles, timing, or a driving loop of its own. A driver calls its methods in the right order and supplies memory access itself. This is the one place ISA semantics live, shared unmodified by both models below, so a bug fix or new instruction benefits both.

Decode dispatch and trap handling follow Appendix C's ISP pseudocode closely, with section citations throughout the source. See SPARC V8 Architecture for the section-by-section mapping.

Also part of it: Decoder (instruction word to Opcode), FloatingPointFunctions.h (IEEE-754 arithmetic), and CoreLogger (SparcCore::logger, which formats and emits the core's state as a trace of architectural events, viewable in the log viewer). Both models below produce the identical trace format.

  • cpp_model SparcStateMachine drives it through an ordinary fetch-decode-execute-trap loop, with zero modeled latency. Every instruction completes in the iteration it starts.
  • sitar_model SparcThread drives it through Sitar, with real per-opcode and memory-access timing.

docs.title: Mmu
docs.text:
A Memory Management Unit (MMU) sits between the core and physical memory, translating the virtual addresses instructions generate into physical addresses, and enforcing the access permissions recorded in an in-memory page table. Present only in core_mmu and later configurations that include an MMU.

This project implements the SPARC Reference MMU, the suggested (not mandatory) MMU design described in Appendix H: a 3-level page table, a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB, the manual's own term for it is Page Descriptor Cache), MMU control/context/fault registers addressed through the ASI mechanism, and referenced/modified (R/M) bit tracking in each page-table entry.

What the model implements:

  • The full page-table walk (all 3 levels, terminating early on a valid leaf or a fault).
  • TLB lookup, with a configurable size and associativity per level, and TLB fill on a miss.
  • R/M bit write-back on a successful translated access.
  • The register map (control, context table pointer, context, fault status, fault address).
  • Probe and flush handling, and the explicit MMU bypass ASI range.

See model/cpp_common_code/mmu/README.md for the full detail.

  • cpp_model MmuCore, a plain C++ class with no notion of cycles or timing, is called directly, the same way MemCore is called in core_only.
  • sitar_model Mmu wraps that same MmuCore class, driving its step-by-step primitives (walk one page-table level, fill the TLB, write back R/M) through real, timed physical accesses instead of one instant call. SparcThread talks to it over the same procedure handshake used for memory in core_only. Below the MMU, physical memory is reached over real Sitar nets. See Model Configurations for the block diagram.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
The model's backing store for main memory. Two implementations exist, depending on configuration:

  • MemCore Flat, byte-addressed, virtual-address-shaped. Used directly by core_only.

  • MainMemory Physical-address-shaped (64-bit/doubleword), used only where an MMU is present. Wraps a MemCore internally and does the doubleword/half-select adaptation itself.

  • cpp_model Called directly, with zero modeled latency.

  • sitar_model VirtualMainMemory (core_only) or PhysicalMainMemory (core_mmu and every later configuration) wraps it with Sitar timing. PhysicalMainMemory is a module, reached over nets rather than a procedure handshake.

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
Split instruction and data L1 caches, between the core and the MMU, in core_l1cache_mmu_devices. Both are virtually indexed and virtually tagged (VIVT): they are looked up with the virtual address, before any translation, which is what lets them sit above the MMU. Their main properties:

  • Organization 64-byte lines. By default 512 lines (32 KB) per cache, direct mapped. Both size and associativity are run-time options (--icache-lines, --icache-ways, --dcache-lines, --dcache-ways). Replacement is round-robin within a set. The MMU context is part of every tag, so the same virtual address in two contexts is two different lines.
  • What is cached Ordinary instruction and data accesses (ASIs 8 to B) to pages the MMU says are cacheable. Everything else (MMU registers, the bypass ASIs) goes straight to the MMU. Device registers are never cached.
  • Reads A hit is served by the cache, provided the page's access permissions (kept with the line) allow it. A miss reads the whole line through the MMU.
  • Writes Write-through: every store also goes to memory at once. A store miss then brings the line into the cache (write-allocate). An atomic load-store bypasses the cache, and updates a cached copy of its line.
  • Flushes Always of a whole cache: a store with ASI 0x10 to 0x14 flushes both caches, 0x18 to 0x1C the instruction cache, the FLUSH instruction both, and a write to the MMU's registers (except the context register) both.
  • Not coherent The caches do not see memory changed behind their back, for example by a bypass store, so a program that does that must flush first (see validation/C/caches/stale_until_flush). In particular, self-modifying code must execute FLUSH before running the new instructions, as the SPARC manual requires.

The C++ class L1CachesCore (model/cpp_common_code/cache/) holds both caches and the whole policy, the same class in both models:

  • cpp_model Called directly between SparcStateMachine and the MMU, with zero modeled latency.
  • sitar_model L1Caches.sitar runs the same steps, with each downstream access a real, timed transaction with the MMU.

docs.title: Peripheral Devices
docs.text: A Timer, a multi-thread Interrupt Controller, and a Serial device, one shared set on the memory side of the MMU. The C++ class PeripheralDevicesCore (model/cpp_common_code/devices/) holds all three, the same class in both models. In the sitar_model the PeripheralDevices module wraps it, reached through the SystemBridge over nets. See Peripheral Devices for the register-level detail.

docs.title: System bus
docs.text:
From core_mmu_devices on, more than one thing sits below the MMU, so a bus routes each physical access by its address: to main memory, to the devices, or (in sparc_apara) to the APARA engine. Which address belongs to which target is defined once, in SystemAddressMap.h, and shared by both models, so the two can never disagree.

  • cpp_model SystemBus, a plain C++ class, called directly, with zero modeled latency.
  • sitar_model SystemBridge, a module with one master (the core), carries one transaction at a time. sparc_apara uses SystemInterconnect instead, the same bus with several masters (the core and the APARA engine's host side), served round robin.

docs.title: APARA Engine
docs.text:
A four-threaded vector compute engine, with its own instruction and data memories, designed to work alongside a SPARC processor as an accelerator. It is modeled in the apara configuration on its own and in sparc_apara next to the SPARC core. As for the SPARC, one C++ class (AparaCore) holds its state and executes its instructions in both models, and the sitar_model adds one module per pipeline stage. See The APARA Accelerator section, and The code there for its classes and modules.

All component-wise timing configurations are listed in Model Configuration Settings.

docs.title: Model Components Reference
docs.text:
A complete, per-file index of every Sitar design unit (module or procedure) in this repo. For each one it lists what it is, where it lives, what plain C++ class (if any) it wraps, what design unit embeds it, and its one-line description. See Model Components for the narrative overview this table indexes. See each file's own header comment for the full detail behind its one-line description here.

There is one table per configuration, listed top-down: the root module first, then its children in the order each parent instantiates them, depth-first. A design unit shared by several configurations (everything under sitar_component_models/) appears in the table of each configuration that uses it. From core_mmu_devices on, each table lists only what differs from the configuration it builds on.

  • Scope common means the file lives in model/sitar_component_models/ and is translated into every configuration's build, whether or not that configuration actually instantiates it. See that folder's own build-script comment. A configuration's name (core_only, core_mmu, ...) means the file lives under that configuration's own system_models/<config>/sitar_model/src/.

  • Parent Names what instantiates this row within the current table's configuration, and how many instances. Reads "None (root)" for Top.

Owns 5 VirtualMainMemoryInterface instances for ifetch, load, store, atomic, and flush. VirtualMainMemoryInterface (procedure) VirtualMainMemoryInterface.sitar common None SparcThread (5 instances: ifetchProcedure, memReadProcedure, memWriteProcedure, atomicLoadStoreProcedure, flushProcedure) Blocking, VM-shaped (VirtualMemoryRequest/Response) memory-access interface. One run per access. Reused across calls. Mmu (procedure) Mmu.sitar common MmuCore Core (1 instance: mmu) The Sitar timing model for the MMU. Sits between SparcThread and physical memory. Drives MmuCore's step-primitives through real, timed physical accesses. PhysicalMainMemoryInterface (procedure) PhysicalMainMemoryInterface.sitar common None Mmu (2 instances: phyMemReadProcedure, phyMemWriteProcedure) Mmu's own physical-access transaction procedure. Nests one PushAToken/PullAToken pair to reach PhysicalMainMemory over nets. PullAToken (procedure) PullAToken.sitar common None PhysicalMainMemoryInterface (1 instance: getPhyMemResponse) and PhysicalMainMemory (1 instance: getRequest) Generic single-token consumer, parameterized by width. Retry-pulls from an inport until it receives exactly one token. PushAToken (procedure) PushAToken.sitar common None PhysicalMainMemoryInterface (1 instance: sendPhyMemRequest) and PhysicalMainMemory (1 instance: sendResponse) Generic single-token producer, parameterized by width. Retry-pushes one token onto an outport until there's room. PhysicalMainMemory (module) PhysicalMainMemory.sitar common MainMemory System (1 instance: mainMemory) Persistent PM-shaped memory model wrapping MainMemory. core_mmu's terminal memory node, below the MMU, reached over nets rather than a procedure handshake.

docs.title: apara
docs.text:
The standalone engine: none of the SPARC design units above take part.

Design unit File Scope Embedded C++ class Parent Description Top (module) Top.sitar apara None None (root) The root module for the apara build. Instantiates one AparaEngine, stops the simulation once every started thread has stopped, and holds the engine's timing knobs. AparaEngine (module) AparaEngine.sitar common None Top (1 instance: engine) The engine's five-stage pipeline: one module per stage, joined by nets with the hardware's channel depths. AparaFetch (module) AparaFetch.sitar common AparaTiming.h (BranchTargetBuffer) AparaEngine (1 instance: fetch) The FETCH stage. Keeps each thread's fetch PC and the branch target buffer, picks a thread round robin, and sends the bundles of its IMEM line to DECODE, one per cycle, each with a predicted next PC. AparaDecode (module) AparaDecode.sitar common None AparaEngine (1 instance: decode) The DECODE stage. Finds a bundle's registers, latency, and divider use, and passes it on its thread's channel to REGFILE. AparaRegfile (module) AparaRegfile.sitar common None AparaEngine (1 instance: regfile) The REGFILE stage. Holds one bundle per thread, issues one per cycle whose registers are unlocked while a token is free, and releases locks and tokens as results come back from EXEC. Also counts, independently of the locks, the bundles issued while a register they read still has a write outstanding (the hazard count), and has the interlock knob that turns the locks off for that check. AparaExec (module) AparaExec.sitar common AparaCore AparaEngine (1 instance: exec) The EXEC stage, and the owner of the engine's functional state. Executes each bundle and holds it for its latency, and checks that the registers it used were within its lock masks. In a system, also serves the host side's requests and sends the engine's loads and stores that leave its data memory. AparaWriteback (module) AparaWriteback.sitar common None AparaEngine (1 instance: writeback) The WRITEBACK stage. Sends FETCH a PC correction for a mispredicted bundle, and a notice when a thread stops.

docs.text:
Every core_l1cache_mmu_devices design unit appears here too, except that this configuration's own System and Core replace those, and SystemInterconnect replaces SystemBridge. The engine's design units are those of apara above (except its Top), plus AparaHost.

Design unit File Scope Embedded C++ class Parent Description System (module) System.sitar sparc_apara None Top Assembles Core, SystemInterconnect, PhysicalMainMemory, PeripheralDevices, AparaEngine, and AparaHost. Owns the consolidated latency-knob block for this configuration, the engine's knobs included. Core (module) Core.sitar sparc_apara None System (1 instance: core) The same as core_l1cache_mmu_devices' Core. SystemInterconnect (module) SystemInterconnect.sitar common None (uses SystemAddressMap.h) System (1 instance: interconnect) The physical bus with two masters, the core and the engine's host side, taken round robin. Routes each request to main memory, the devices, or the engine's windows, one transaction at a time. AparaEngine (module) AparaEngine.sitar common None System (1 instance: engine) As in apara. AparaHost (module) AparaHost.sitar common AparaControlCore, AparaDmaCore System (1 instance: host) The engine's host side: its control unit and DMA unit. Serves the SPARC's accesses to the engine's three windows, carries out their commands through engine.exec, and sends DMA transfers and the engine's outside loads and stores onto the bus as its second master. Drives the engine's interrupt.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Module vs. procedure Top, System, Core, PhysicalMainMemory, SystemBridge, SystemInterconnect, PeripheralDevices, and every Apara* design unit are modules. Every other row above is a procedure. See the sibling sitar repo's own documentation for the general module/procedure distinction, and System.sitar's own header comment for how it plays out in core_mmu specifically.

  • Reading "None" in the C++ class column This applies to every request/response-only or token-only procedure (VirtualMainMemoryInterface, PhysicalMainMemoryInterface, PullAToken, PushAToken), to the three purely structural modules (Top, System, Core), to the buses (SystemBridge, SystemInterconnect), and to the APARA pipeline stages that only move bundles (AparaEngine, AparaDecode, AparaRegfile, AparaWriteback). None of these hold a functional-model class instance themselves.

docs.title: Model Configuration Settings
docs.text:
The C++ only models (cpp_model/) offer pure functionality modeling. An instruction "completes" the moment it starts, with no notion of how long it would actually take on real hardware. The Sitar models (sitar_model/) additionally offer component-wise latency modeling: independent, configurable delay values for opcode execution, each memory-access channel, and, where present, the MMU and its interconnect to physical memory, the caches, the devices, and the APARA engine.

Some of the settings below are structural: they change what the model does, e.g. how many TLB entries exist. Others are timing: they change how long something takes, with no effect on the functional result. Some can only be changed at compile time (edit a header, rebuild). Others are ordinary runtime fields, given an initial value in a configuration's own init block, but otherwise no different from any other piece of simulation state, settable at any later point too, e.g. with a debugger (see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB) or from scripted Sitar behavior code.

docs.title: Where to set
docs.text:
Most of the timing knobs below are consolidated in one place per configuration, alongside the wiring that connects the pieces they belong to: Core.sitar's own init block for core_only, or System.sitar's for core_mmu and any later configuration assembled the same way (and Top.sitar's for apara, which has no System). Structural knobs each live in their own compile-time header instead, listed individually below.

The timing parameters below apply only to the Sitar-timed models (sitar_model/). The C++ only models (cpp_model/) have no notion of cycles at all, so timing knobs have no effect on them. Structural parameters apply to both.

These settings apply only to configurations that include an MMU: core_mmu, core_mmu_devices, core_l1cache_mmu_devices, and sparc_apara. In each of them, the runtime knobs below live in that configuration's own System.sitar (the links below are to core_mmu's).

The engine's own settings. Each runtime knob is set in one place per configuration: Top.sitar in apara, System.sitar in sparc_apara. See APARA Timing Model for what each one models.

docs.title: Model Configurations
docs.text:
This project provides several system configurations.

  • core_only Models only the SPARC core connected to main memory. Every processor-generated address (a virtual address) is used directly to index into main memory, with no translation.
  • core_mmu Adds a Memory Management Unit (MMU) between the core and main memory. Every processor-generated virtual address is translated to a physical address before it reaches main memory.
  • core_mmu_devices Adds a timer, an interrupt controller, and a serial device, as one shared set on the memory side of the MMU, reached by physical address like main memory.
  • core_l1cache_mmu_devices Adds split instruction and data L1 caches between the core and the MMU. VIVT and write-through.

Two more configurations model the APARA accelerator, a vector compute engine designed to work alongside a SPARC processor: apara, one engine on its own, and sparc_apara, core_l1cache_mmu_devices plus one engine, which the SPARC program loads, starts, and exchanges data with. They are described in their own section, The APARA Accelerator.

For each configuration, there exist two implementations:

  • cpp_model A 0-delay functional model. A plain host C++ function-call chain through the model's components, with no notion of cycles or timing.
  • sitar_model A cycle-timed model. The same components, driven through Sitar with real per-opcode, interconnect, and memory timing.

The configurations and their path in the project (linked) are summarized here:

Configuration Type Description core_only cpp (functional model) The core plus main memory. No MMU, devices, or caches. core_only sitar (timing model) The core plus main memory. No MMU, devices, or caches. core_mmu cpp (functional model) Adds an MMU between the core and main memory. core_mmu sitar (timing model) Adds an MMU between the core and main memory. core_mmu_devices cpp (functional model) Adds the peripheral devices below the MMU. core_mmu_devices sitar (timing model) Adds the peripheral devices below the MMU. core_l1cache_mmu_devices cpp (functional model) Adds split L1 caches between the core and the MMU. core_l1cache_mmu_devices sitar (timing model) Adds split L1 caches between the core and the MMU. apara cpp (functional model) One APARA engine on its own, no SPARC core. See The APARA Engine. apara sitar (timing model) One APARA engine on its own, with its pipeline's timing. sparc_apara cpp (functional model) core_l1cache_mmu_devices plus one APARA engine. See The Engine in a System. sparc_apara sitar (timing model) core_l1cache_mmu_devices plus one APARA engine, on a two-master bus.

For each configuration, both the cpp and sitar models include the same components: core_mmu's MMU, for example, is present in both its cpp_model and its sitar_model, just reached with 0 added delay in the former and real Sitar timing in the latter.

See Model Components for the list of all components, such as the SPARC Core, the MMU, and devices, that are included in this project.

Each configuration's folder also has a COMPONENTS file, listing what it contains, so that the validation runner knows which test suites it can run (see Validation Suite).

docs.text: For specifically the Sitar models, which have a notion of structure and timing, this section describes the structure and component interconnections for each configuration, as well as the code structure.

docs.text: No net crossing anywhere. The core talks directly to memory over a procedure handshake, so zero delay communication is possible between the core and memory procedures. The "--||--" symbol indicates direct communication between the two procedures using a handshake and shared variables.

docs.title: Structure diagram
docs.text:
The core and its MMU are unchanged from core_mmu. Below the MMU sits a bridge, which reads the physical address of each access and sends it either to main memory or to the peripheral devices (Timer, Serial, Interrupt Controller). The devices are one shared set on the memory side, not part of the core. That is what lets several cores share them later.

Every arrow between modules is a net, and every net crossing costs at least one cycle. A memory access crosses four nets here (core to bridge to memory, and back), two more than in core_mmu. The Interrupt Controller sends its interrupt level to the core over its own net, as a level: a token arrives only when the level changes, and the core polls that net once per cycle. An interrupt therefore reaches the core one cycle after the Interrupt Controller raises it.

The devices' behavior is the same C++ class in both models (PeripheralDevicesCore). The cpp_model ticks it once after every core cycle. The sitar_model's PeripheralDevices module ticks it once per simulated cycle. See Peripheral Devices for what the devices do.

docs.text:
The same system as core_mmu_devices, with one more procedure inside Core: the split L1 caches, between sparcThread and mmu. All three are procedures of the one Core module, so a cache hit completes with no net crossing and no added delay (unless a hit-latency knob is set). A miss reads the whole 64-byte line through the MMU, which costs the MMU's translation plus eight doubleword transactions through the bridge. See Model Components for what the caches do.

Nothing is cached while the MMU is disabled, unless the MMU Control Register's "always cacheable" bit is set. A program can set it itself, or the simulator can, with --always-cacheable.

docs.text:
APARA is a vector compute engine designed to work alongside a SPARC processor as an accelerator. These pages cover the engine on its own (apara) and next to the SPARC core (sparc_apara).

docs.title: Performance Modeling
docs.text:
Model configuration knobs are of two kinds, structural and timing. See Model Configuration Settings for the complete list of both kinds, and where to set each one.

Once you've chosen knob values to model a specific system (rebuild first if any of them are compile-time), run the simulation with --stats enabled.

docs.title: Printing the performance measures
docs.text:
Every configuration's own executable, both drivers, takes an optional --stats flag, alongside the existing <hex_file> [expected_file] [max_cycles] arguments (it can appear anywhere among them):

model/system_models/core_mmu/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_mmu <hex> --stats

Off by default, so run_simple_test.sh and validation/run_tests.py run unaffected. When given, it prints every performance measure the model tracks (the table below), to stdout, once the run finishes. Each configuration prints only what it actually has: core_only prints its core statistics alone. core_mmu prints core statistics, then MMU statistics, then physical memory statistics. The later configurations add their caches' and devices' statistics, and, in sparc_apara, the APARA engine's.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of the peripheral devices modeled here is to include a bare minimum set of devices that make the model realistic, and sufficient to port a basic operating system on top of it.

  • Timer A one-shot timer, used for generating periodic interrupts, the kind an OS uses for context switching.
  • Interrupt Controller Routes hardware interrupts to the hardware threads of every core, and lets threads interrupt each other (inter-processor interrupts).
  • Serial Device A single device for I/O.

The register formats, addresses, and behavior documented here are credited to the AJIT processor documentation, Chapter 8, "Basic peripherals available for AJIT systems". The device models in this project are designed to be compatible with it, except for the deviations listed at the end of this page.

docs.title: Connection diagram
docs.text:
A programmer's view of how the devices connect.

There is a single shared set of devices in the system, on the memory side of the MMU. Every device has registers that are read and written over the same physical bus the core uses for main memory, by physical address. In the Sitar model a bridge routes each access to main memory or to the devices (see Model Configurations). Each device also has its own individual signal pins, unrelated to the bus:

  • Timer: a clock_in input, and a timer_int_out output to the Interrupt Controller.
  • Serial Device: serial_in/serial_out pins, and a serial_int_out output to the Interrupt Controller.
  • Interrupt Controller: timer_int_out/serial_int_out inputs, an external interrupt input (env_int_in, for an external source such as an accelerator: in sparc_apara, the APARA engine), and one interrupt_level output per hardware thread. Inter-processor interrupts are generated inside it, from its own IPI registers.

docs.title: Device address map
docs.text:
Reach the registers with the MMU bypass ASI (0x20, see Appendix I of the SPARC V8 manual), or with an ordinary translated access if the page is identity mapped.

Device : Register Address Access type Instruction example Interrupt Controller : Control, thread (core c, thread t) 0xFFFF3000 + 4*(2c+t) word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Interrupt Controller : IPI registers 0xFFFF3080 to 0xFFFF30CB word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Timer : Control 0xFFFF3100 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Control 0xFFFF3200 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Tx 0xFFFF3204 byte (8-bit) stba %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Rx 0xFFFF3208 byte (8-bit) lduba [%rd] 0x20, %rs Serial : Baud limit / baud control 0xFFFF320c word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20 Serial : Baud frequency 0xFFFF3210 word (32-bit) sta %rs, [%rd] 0x20

%rd holds the register's address, loaded with set beforehand. C programs can use the routines in compiler/include/ instead (see C Programs).

An access to an address in the device window (0xFFFF0000 and up) that no device decodes reads as 0 and ignores writes, with a warning from the simulator.

docs.title: Interrupt levels
docs.text:
Source IRL Priority Timer 10 Highest IPI (inter-processor interrupt) 11 Serial 12 Env (external: the APARA engine in sparc_apara) 14 Lowest

For each hardware thread, the Interrupt Controller priority-encodes the active sources that thread's mask enables: the lowest IRL number among them wins. See the Interrupt Controller page for the details.

docs.title: Deviations from the AJIT Processor
docs.text:
Differences from AJIT's own device models (in its multi-core C model, devices/src/ in the ajit-toolchain repository), each small and deliberate:

  • Timer clock. AJIT's timer counts wall-clock time on the host. Here it counts model ticks, one per core cycle by default (a configurable divider). In hardware the timer may run off its own clock, so timer counts are not hardware time.
  • IPI register decode. AJIT decodes the IPI word index from the low 6 address bits only, so its last three IPI words alias onto the first three (the lock word lands on thread 0's message). Here all 19 words are separate.
  • Serial baud registers and UART_reset. Present here (from the AJIT processor description), absent from AJIT's C model. The baud values are stored and read back but do not set the model's transmit timing, which is its own knob.
  • Serial receive disable. Writing Rx_en=0 disables the receiver from any state here, as the AJIT processor description says. AJIT's C model only does so while holding a received byte.
  • Serial transmit disable. Writing Tx_en=0 while a byte is still being transmitted finishes sending it first, so no program output is lost.
  • Unmapped device addresses read as 0 and ignore writes, with a warning, the same as AJIT's bridge does for any unmapped address.
  • Device map and C routines. The address map above is AJIT's default device map, so software written for AJIT finds every device where it expects it. The headers in compiler/include/ keep the file names, function names, and signatures of AJIT's bare-metal access routines (tools/ajit_access_routines_mt/ in the ajit-toolchain repository), so code written for AJIT compiles here unchanged; the implementations are this project's own.
  • Serial register addresses. The map above is the one in the multi-thread access routines (tools/ajit_access_routines_mt/include/default_device_addresses.h, ajit-toolchain repository, marshal branch). Older AJIT sources (the single-thread access routines, AJIT's C models, and the processor description's Serial chapter) put Tx at 0xFFFF3210 and Rx at 0xFFFF3220.

docs.title: Interrupt Controller
docs.text:
A single, shared Interrupt Controller (IRC) routes the system's interrupt sources to the hardware threads of every core. It has two parts:

  • one slot per hardware thread, each with its own control register, its own state, and its own interrupt_level output to that thread;
  • an inter-processor interrupt (IPI) block, which lets any thread interrupt any other (or itself).

All its registers are accessed with word loads and stores. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

docs.title: Interrupt sources
docs.text:
Source IRL Reaches Timer 10 every slot (each slot's mask decides) IPI 11 the destination slot only Serial Device 12 every slot (each slot's mask decides) External (env_int_in) 14 every slot (each slot's mask decides)

The external input is for a source outside this device set, such as an accelerator. In sparc_apara the APARA engine drives it, to signal that an engine thread or a DMA transfer has finished (see The Engine in a System). In the other configurations nothing drives it, and it stays 0.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text: There are 8 slots, enough for 4 cores with 2 hardware threads each. The slot for core c, thread t is number 2c + t, and its control register is at 0xFFFF3000 + 4*(2c + t). A program finds its own core and thread with rd %asr29, which reads (core << 8) | thread (in C, ajit_get_core_and_thread_id()). The single-core configurations here are core 0, thread 0, so they use slot 0 at 0xFFFF3000.

docs.title: Control register
docs.text:
Bits Field Access Description [0] Enable read/write 1 enables this slot. Writing 0 disables it and drops its interrupt_level. [15:1] Level mask read/write Bit i set: interrupt level i is delivered to this thread. [30:16] Active sources read only Bit 15+i is 1 while a source at level i is active, whether or not it is masked. [31] Interrupting read only 1 while the slot is in IRC_INTERRUPTING.

The mask bit positions equal each source's level, so masking a source is a bitwise AND. Writes to the read-only bits are ignored. The active sources field lets software see a source that is pending but masked, and is readable even while the slot is disabled.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: When more than one enabled level is active at once, the lowest level number wins: Timer (10) > IPI (11) > Serial (12) > External (14).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each slot runs its own state machine:

  • IRC_DISABLED The reset state. interrupt_level is 0. A write that sets the enable bit moves to IRC_ENABLED.
  • IRC_ENABLED Watches the sources. As soon as any level enabled in the mask is active, interrupt_level is set to that level (the highest-priority one, if more than one), and the slot moves to IRC_INTERRUPTING.
  • IRC_INTERRUPTING interrupt_level stays asserted, even if the source goes away, until software clears the enable bit.

A write that clears the enable bit, from any state, immediately drops interrupt_level and moves to IRC_DISABLED. A write that sets the enable bit while already enabled or interrupting only updates the mask.

docs.title: Handling an interrupt
docs.text:
The usual sequence, which the routines in compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h implement (see C Programs):

  1. The interrupt trap for level L is taken.
  2. The handler disables its own slot, which drops interrupt_level.
  3. It clears the source (for example, disables the timer, or reads the Serial device's Rx register).
  4. It enables its slot again. If another enabled source is still active, the slot delivers it next.

docs.title: Inter-processor interrupts (IPI)
docs.text:
The IPI block is 19 words at 0xFFFF3080:

Offset Register Description 0x00 IPI mask Bit s: IPIs to slot s are enabled. 0x04 IPI value Bit s: an IPI is pending for slot s. 0x08 to 0x47 Messages 8 bytes per destination slot (slot s at 0x08 + 8s), for software. 0x48 Lock A word for software to use as a lock.

Slot s sees an IPI (level 11) while bit s is set in both the mask and the value. To interrupt another thread, a thread writes a message for it, then sets its bit in the value register (and in the mask, if not already set). The interrupted thread reads its message and clears its value bit. Locking around these steps, with the lock word or otherwise, is up to software. The routines in compiler/include/ajit_ipi.h (__ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__() and friends) do the register work.

docs.title: Serial Device
docs.text:
A memory-mapped serial device (UART) that exchanges bytes between the core and an external I/O device. It has serial_in/serial_out pins, a serial_int_out output pin to the Interrupt Controller (IRL 12), and communicates with the core over the shared address/data bus through its own set of registers. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

A single instance is modeled. A self-tuning variant, which auto-detects baud rate from an initial calibration byte, is not used here.

docs.title: Registers
docs.text:
Register Width Access Control 32-bit word (ld/st) Tx 8-bit byte store (stb), write only Rx 8-bit byte load (ldub), read only Baud limit / baud control 32-bit word Baud frequency 32-bit word

See Peripheral Devices for the address of each register.

Each register has its own address. Tx and Rx are byte registers: a byte store to Tx's address sends that byte, and a byte load from Rx's address returns the received byte.

docs.title: Control register bit-fields
docs.text: Bit Field Description [0] Tx_en Transmit enable. [1] Rx_en Receive enable. [2] Rx_interrupt_enable If set, receiving a byte raises an interrupt. [3] Tx_full (read-only) Set once the CPU writes Tx, cleared once it is transmitted. [4] Rx_full (read-only) Set once a byte is received into Rx, cleared once the CPU reads it. [5] UART_reset Writing 1 resets both state machines to their reset state (a byte still being transmitted is dropped). Always reads 0.

docs.title: Baud rate
docs.text:
The baud-limit and baud-frequency registers are computed from a desired baud rate and clock frequency, from the GCD of 16 times the baud rate and the clock frequency:

gcd            = GCD(16 x baud_rate, clock_frequency)
baud_frequency = (16 x baud_rate) / gcd
baud_limit     = (clock_frequency / gcd) - baud_frequency

The model stores both registers and reads them back, but they do not set its transmit timing. How long a byte takes to transmit is the model's own txTicksPerByte setting (default 1 cycle, see Model Configuration Settings).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The device is modeled by two independent state machines, transmit and receive, sharing the one control register above.

docs.title: Transmit
docs.text:
• TX_DISABLED The reset state. A write of Tx_en=1 clears Tx_full and moves to TX_ENABLED.
  • TX_ENABLED Waits for a Tx register write. On one, Tx_full is set and the device moves to TX_TRANSMITTING.
  • TX_TRANSMITTING Once the byte finishes transmitting, Tx_full is cleared and the device returns to TX_ENABLED. A Tx write while still transmitting is dropped.

A write of Tx_en=0 from any state returns to TX_DISABLED. If a byte is still being transmitted, it is sent first.

To send a byte: enable the transmitter, write the byte to the Tx register, then poll Tx_full until it clears before writing the next one (or disable the transmitter).

docs.title: Receive
docs.text:
• RX_DISABLED The reset state. A write of Rx_en=1 clears Rx_full and moves to RX_ENABLED.
  • RX_ENABLED Waits for a byte on the serial_in pin. On one, Rx_full is set, an interrupt is raised if Rx_interrupt_enable is set, and the device moves to RX_DATA_RECEIVED.
  • RX_DATA_RECEIVED Once the CPU reads the Rx register, Rx_full and the interrupt are cleared and the device returns to RX_ENABLED.

A write of Rx_en=0 from any state clears Rx_full and the interrupt, and returns to RX_DISABLED. While the receiver is disabled or still holds an unread byte, incoming bytes wait, they are not lost.

The receiver supports two usage modes, selected by Rx_interrupt_enable:

  • Polling mode (Rx_interrupt_enable=0): enable the receiver, poll Rx_full until it sets, then read the Rx register (and disable the receiver, or leave it enabled for the next byte).
  • Interrupt mode (Rx_interrupt_enable=1): enable the receiver, wait for the interrupt, then read the Rx register (and disable the receiver, or leave it enabled for the next byte).

docs.title: Where the bytes go in the simulator
docs.text:
The serial device exists so a program can show output and take input. By default every transmitted byte is written straight to the simulator's own standard output, as the program sends it. Received bytes come from an input file. Every configuration with devices accepts:

Option Effect --serial-in <file> Bytes received on serial_in come from this file, in order. --serial-out <file> Transmitted bytes go to this file instead of standard output. --serial-pty A pseudo-terminal carries both directions. The simulator prints its device name, attach any terminal program to it.

Without --serial-in, a file next to the program's .hex with the same name and the extension .serial_in is used, if it exists. That is how a validation test carries its own input.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text: A simple timer that operates only in one-shot mode. It has a clock_in input pin, a timer_int_out output pin to the Interrupt Controller, and communicates with the core over the shared address/data bus through a single control register, accessed with word load/stores only. See Peripheral Devices for the connection diagram and the full address map.

docs.title: Control register
docs.text:
Bits Field Description [0] Timer_en Enable bit. Writing 1 starts the timer, writing 0 disables it. [31:1] Timer_max_count The number of ticks to count, set on the same write that enables the timer.

A read of the Control register returns it as last written. The live count is not readable. Byte stores update only the bytes they select.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Software writes a maximum count into the control register and sets the enable bit in the same write. From that point, the timer counts clock_in edges, starting from 0. When the count reaches the maximum, the timer asserts its interrupt output (IRL 10, see Peripheral Devices) and stops counting. A maximum count of 0 or 1 both fire on the first edge. The interrupt output stays asserted until software explicitly disables the timer.

In the simulator, one clock_in edge is one core cycle by default. A divider makes it every n cycles instead (--timer-tick-divider <n>, or the timerTickDivider setting, see Model Configuration Settings). In hardware the timer may run off a different clock than the core, so timer counts here are model ticks, not hardware time.

  • TIMER_DISABLED The reset state. The interrupt output is 0. A write of Timer_en=1 clears the count, captures Timer_max_count, and moves to TIMER_ENABLED.
  • TIMER_ENABLED Counts up. The interrupt output is 0. When the count reaches Timer_max_count, the interrupt output is asserted, and the timer moves to TIMER_INTERRUPTING. A further write of Timer_en=1 does not restart it.
  • TIMER_INTERRUPTING The timer stops counting. The interrupt output stays asserted until the CPU writes Timer_en=0, which clears it and returns the timer to TIMER_DISABLED.

A write of Timer_en=0 from any state immediately clears the count and the interrupt output, and moves to TIMER_DISABLED.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: A free running 64-bit counter across ASR[31] and ASR[30], running at the processor clock and read-only, is documented separately from this Timer. It is unrelated to it, a CPU-internal cycle counter rather than a memory-mapped, software-configured timer. Our Sitar model does not yet implement this counter.

docs.title: SPARC V8 Architecture
docs.text:
SPARC (Scalable Processor ARChitecture) is a RISC instruction set architecture originally developed at Sun Microsystems, derived from the Berkeley RISC I/II research designs. SPARC V8 is the 32-bit revision of this architecture, standardized as ANSI/IEEE Std 1754-1994. See the Wikipedia SPARC article for general background and history.

SPARC's most distinctive architectural feature is a register window file. A procedure call can get a fresh set of registers without spilling to memory, simply by advancing a circular window into a larger physical register file.

The authoritative specification is The SPARC Architecture Manual, Version 8, included in this repository. This project's model follows it closely, with section references cited throughout the source (model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp in particular).

docs.title: Why this page exists
docs.text:
The manual PDF has no hyperlinked table of contents or bookmarks of its own, so jumping to a specific chapter or section means scrolling through 295 pages by hand. Every entry in the tables below links directly to that chapter, appendix, or section's own starting page in the bundled PDF.

Page numbers below are the manual's own printed page numbers (the ones in each page's footer, also what this project's own source comments cite), not the PDF file's raw page count. The two drift apart by the end of the document.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: Chapter Title What it's about Pages 1 Introduction What SPARC is, its design goals and principal features, and how conformance/compliance is defined. 1-8 2 Overview The architecture end to end, briefly: registers, instruction categories, traps, memory. The best single starting point for a first read. 9-16 3 Data Formats Integer, floating-point (single/double/quad), and tagged-arithmetic data formats. 17-22 4 Registers The register file and windowing mechanism in full detail, PSR/WIM/TBR and every other state register. 23-42 5 Instructions The instruction set itself: formats, addressing modes, every opcode. 43-58 6 Memory Model Total Store Ordering (TSO) and Partial Store Ordering (PSO), and what ordering guarantees software can rely on. 59-68 7 Traps Trap handling, priorities, and the trap table, directly relevant to how every test program in this repository halts. See Writing and Running Assembly Programs. 69-80
