The reference to look an opcode up in. 87-150 C ISP Descriptions The same instructions again, but as precise pseudocode (ISP notation). This is what model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp implements almost line for line, see the table below. 151-188 D Software Considerations Conventions and assumptions a compiler or operating system can rely on, e.g. register-window overflow/underflow handling. 189-204 E Example Integer Multiplication and Division Routines Worked software routines for multiply/divide/remainder, for implementations that don't have them in hardware. 205-226 F Opcodes and Condition Codes Tables of every opcode's bit encoding and every condition code's meaning. Handy as a quick lookup alongside Appendix B. 227-232 G SPARC ABI Software Considerations The calling convention and binary-compatibility rules SPARC application binaries follow. 233-240 H SPARC Reference MMU Architecture A suggested (not mandatory) MMU design. See Model Components. 241-268 J Programming with the Memory Model An intuitive, example-driven companion to Chapter 6's memory model. 269-280 K Formal Specification of the Memory Model The same memory model again, stated formally and precisely. 281-288 L Implementation Characteristics How specific historical SPARC chips actually implemented the architecture, including which instructions they left unimplemented in hardware. 289-296 M Instruction Set Summary A compact, one-line-per-instruction summary table of the entire instruction set. 297-298 N SPARC IEEE 754 Implementation Recommendations How the floating-point unit should handle IEEE 754 details the standard itself leaves open. 299-303

docs.title: Appendix C in detail
docs.text:
Appendix C is the one this project's core implementation (model/cpp_common_code/SparcCore.cpp) cites most, its section numbers appear directly in source comments throughout that file and model/cpp_common_code/SparcStateMachine.cpp.

Section Title What it's about Page C.1 ISP Notation The pseudocode notation itself, adapted from Bell and Newell's 1971 ISP notation. 151 C.2 Processor External Interface Definition The signals and macros the rest of Appendix C's pseudocode is built from. 152 C.3 Register Field Definitions How register bit-fields are named and addressed in the pseudocode that follows. 154 C.4 Instruction Field Definitions How instruction-word bit-fields (op, rd, rs1, simm13, and so on) are named in the pseudocode that follows. 156 C.5 Processor States and Instruction Dispatch The top-level execute_mode/reset_mode/error_mode state machine and fetch-decode-execute-trap loop. SparcStateMachine::runOneCycle() implements this loop directly. 156 C.6 Instruction Dispatch The dispatch_instruction macro: how an instruction is routed to integer, FPop, or CPop execution. 159 C.7 Floating-point Execution The complete_fp_execution macro: floating-point trap checks and the Floating-point State Register (FSR). 160 C.8 Traps The execute_trap macro: how the highest-priority pending trap is selected and dispatched. SparcCore::executeTraps() implements this. 161 C.9 Instruction Definitions The ISP pseudocode for every instruction, one by one. This is the definition each SparcCore::execute_*() function follows. 163 C.10 Floating-Point Operate Instructions Notation specific to the multiple-precision floating-point instructions (register-pair/quad alignment). 184

docs.title: Validation Suite
docs.text:
Validating a processor model can mean different things: functional (does each instruction do the right thing), timing or microarchitectural (does it take the right number of cycles, in the right order), or both. This project's SPARC suite, in validation/asm/ and validation/C/, is purely functional. There are no SPARC timing tests here. Both models drive the exact same SparcCore (see Models), so this one suite validates both, and catches a regression in either.

It checks the core's instruction-level behavior against the SPARC V8 manual, in two ways:

  • validation/asm/, hand-written assembly, each test targeting one instruction (or a small family of closely related ones) in isolation.
  • validation/C/, compiled from freestanding C, each test a small self-validating program (a sort, an FFT, a checksum) exercising many instructions together the way a real program would.

It consists of two things: the tests themselves (see "What's in a test" below), and a script, validation/run_tests.py, that runs them all and prints a pass/fail summary (see "The validation script" below).

Beside the SPARC suite, further suites test the components of the larger configurations: the MMU, the peripheral devices, the caches, and the APARA engine, both on its own (with timing tests too) and driven by a SPARC program. Each suite runs only on the configurations that have its components (see Which tests run on which configuration).

This page covers how a test is put together, how to run the suite, and how to add a new one. For actually writing a test program (the trap table, the pass-fail convention, structuring a self-validating C test), see Writing and Running Assembly Programs and Writing and Running C Programs.

docs.title: What's in a test
docs.text:
Every test is a matched set of files sharing one name, for example ADD.s, ADD.hex, ADD.objdump, ADD.vprj, and ADD.expected (validation/asm/integer_alu/Arithmetic/Add/). Only two of these are written by hand:

  • <name>.s or <name>.c, the source program.
  • <name>.vprj, its expected final state, in the human-friendly format described below.

The rest are derived automatically, not hand-written (though .hex and .objdump are still committed as build artifacts, see "The validation script" below for why):

  • <name>.hex, the memory image compiled from the source, loadable directly by either model.
  • <name>.objdump, its disassembly plus full symbol table, useful for finding an address to give gdb, see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB.
  • <name>.expected, the .vprj's checks rewritten into the plain format the checker executables themselves take as a direct command-line argument, see Getting Started.

In short, .vprj is what you write, once, by hand. .expected is what run_tests.py generates from it, fresh, every time the test runs. It's never edited directly, and doesn't need to be committed to git.

docs.title: The .vprj expected-results format
docs.text:
SOURCES = ADD.s

RESULTS =
g1=0x00000080
o0=0x00000005
o2=0xFFFFFFFB
  • SOURCES names the paired .s/.c file.
  • Each RESULTS line is either a register check (<name>=<hex value>, register mnemonics g1-g7, o0-o7, l0-l7, i0-i7, f0-f31, psr, fpsr, y, wim, tbr, pc, npc, asr0-asr31) or a memory check (m[<hex addr>]=<hex value>, a word-aligned 32-bit read).
  • Either kind of line accepts an optional trailing mask (m[0x148] = 0x00000021 0x00000021 checks only the bits set in the mask. See validation/asm/floating_point/fp_exceptions/accrued_inexact.s for a real example distinguishing individual FSR bits.)
  • asi = ... lines are recognized and ignored. MemCore is a single flat address space with no ASI distinction.

Before running a test, run_tests.py parses this and normalizes it into the plain REG <name> <hex value> [mask] / MEM <addr> <hex value> [mask] format, writing it to a .expected file alongside the test.

Four optional lines, used by the device and APARA tests:

  • STARTUP = crt0_interrupts.s, before RESULTS, links that startup file instead of compiler/crt0.s (C tests only).
  • MCODE = kernel.mcode, before RESULTS, names an APARA engine program the test carries, in mcode or in C (MCODE = kernel.c). Before compiling, build_hex.py assembles or compiles it, and writes it out as a C header, kernel.mcode.h (or kernel.c.h), for the test to #include (C tests only, may be repeated). See The Engine in a System.
  • MAX_CYCLES = 1000000, before RESULTS, raises the cycle limit for a test that legitimately runs long (the runner uses the larger of this and its --max-cycles).
  • serial_out = "text", among the results, checks the exact bytes the program sent out through the Serial device (C-style escapes such as \n and \x41 work). Only configurations with devices check it.

A test's received serial input, if it needs any, is a file named after the test with the extension .serial_in, next to its .hex.

docs.title: The validation script
docs.text:
A two-phase pipeline, so the existing suite can be run without a cross-compiler installed at all.

# phase 1 (needs the sparc-elf toolchain): assembles/compiles .s or .c
# into .hex, only needed when you add or edit a test's source
validation/build_hex.py validation

# phase 2: runs the already-built .hex against a model
validation/run_tests.py validation

[PASS] validation/asm/misc/save_restore/SAVE.vprj
[PASS] validation/asm/misc/stbar_unimp_nop_sethi/STBAR_UNIMP_NOP_SETHI.vprj

<passed>/<total> tests passed

Since .hex files are committed to git, phase 2 alone is enough to run the existing suite. Phase 1 is only needed after adding or editing a .s/.c source, and also (re)generates that test's .objdump.

You can point run_tests.py at any subset too, not just the validation root:

validation/run_tests.py validation/asm/floating_point
validation/run_tests.py validation/C

It recurses to find .vprj files, so nesting is free. Tests the configuration cannot run are skipped, and listed at the end (see Which tests run on which configuration).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Does --config NAME Which system_models configuration to run against, default core_only. E.g. --config core_mmu runs against model/system_models/core_mmu/'s own executables instead, and runs only the tests core_mmu can run. --sitar Run against the chosen configuration's Sitar-timed model instead of its plain C++ model (the default). Same CLI, same .vprj format, same PASS/FAIL/OVERALL output either way. See Getting Started to build it. --max-cycles N Per-test cycle limit, default 200,000. A test that hasn't halted by then is reported as a failure, rather than hanging forever on a genuine bug. A "cycle" means one complete instruction executed against the plain C++ model, and an actual clock cycle against the Sitar-timed model, see Getting Started. -v Show every check's result, not just failures. 
validation/run_tests.py validation --config core_mmu --sitar -v
validation/run_tests.py validation/asm/control_transfer --max-cycles 50000

validation/clean.sh [folder] removes generated build byproducts (.o, .elf, .expected) without touching .hex/.s/.c/.vprj/.objdump.

docs.title: Which tests run on which configuration
docs.text:
Not every test can run on every configuration: the MMU tests need an MMU, the APARA tests an engine. Two small files decide which tests a configuration runs, so that you can always point run_tests.py at the whole of validation/:

  • COMPONENTS, in each configuration's folder (model/system_models/<config>/COMPONENTS), lists what the configuration contains.
  • REQUIRES, in a suite's folder, lists what its tests need. Requirements add up down the tree: a test needs everything its own folder's and every parent folder's REQUIRES file lists.

run_tests.py --config <config> runs the tests whose requirements the configuration has, and lists the folders it skipped, with the reason:

skipped 4 test(s) under validation/C/caches: core_only has no caches
skipped 8 test(s) under validation/C/devices: core_only has no devices
skipped 12 test(s) under validation/C/mmu: core_only has no mmu
skipped 108 test(s) under validation/apara: core_only has no apara_standalone
skipped 26 test(s) under validation/sparc_apara: core_only has no apara, devices

241/241 tests passed (158 skipped)

The components, and which configuration has which:

Configuration COMPONENTS core_only sparc core_mmu sparc mmu core_mmu_devices sparc mmu devices core_l1cache_mmu_devices sparc mmu devices caches sparc_apara sparc mmu devices caches apara apara apara_standalone (the engine alone, no SPARC core)

And the suites, with what they require, and where they run:

Folder REQUIRES Runs on asm/, C/ (the benchmarks), test_simple_ADD/ sparc every SPARC configuration C/mmu/ sparc mmu core_mmu and later C/devices/ sparc devices core_mmu_devices and later C/caches/ sparc caches core_l1cache_mmu_devices, sparc_apara sparc_apara/ sparc devices apara sparc_apara apara/ apara_standalone apara, with its own runner, validation/apara/run_tests.py

The engine's own suites, in apara/, are engine programs rather than SPARC programs, so they have their own format and runner (see Writing and Running APARA Programs). run_tests.py --config apara says so, and stops.

A new configuration needs only its COMPONENTS file to work with every existing suite. A new suite that needs more than the SPARC core gets a REQUIRES file.

docs.title: The test collection
docs.text:
The SPARC suite has two sub-suites, side by side under validation/, both using the same .vprj format and the same two-phase pipeline above. The component suites follow in the next section.

  • asm/ Hand-written assembly tests, each targeting one instruction (or a small family of closely related ones, such as every branch condition) in isolation: integer ALU ops, control transfer (branches, traps, call, jump, rett), loads and stores (including atomic and coprocessor variants), and floating point. Organized into category subfolders: integer_alu/, floating_point/, control_transfer/, data_transfer/, misc/. compiler/assemble.sh builds a test's .s into .hex/.objdump, called automatically by build_hex.py above.

  • C/ Self-validating bare-metal C mini-benchmarks, each compiled program exercising a sequence of C-level operations together (loops, arrays, structs, global variables) the way a real program would, rather than one instruction in isolation. compiler/compile_c.sh builds a test's .c the same way. Every test here follows the same shape: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed once on the host machine and hardcoded right there in the source, and report pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0. Its .vprj then only ever has to check o0=1, instead of re-embedding the golden value a second time. See Writing and Running C Programs for the full convention, and array_sum/array_sum.c for a worked example.

    Test What it computes array_sum Sum of a small int array matrix_mul 3x3 integer matrix multiply fft 4-point integer radix-2 FFT root_finding Integer square root via Newton-Raphson integer_sort Bubble sort gcd Euclidean algorithm fibonacci Iterative Fibonacci prime_sieve Sieve of Eratosthenes checksum Byte-array checksum dot_product Integer vector dot product

Alongside them sits test_simple_ADD/, one more .vprj test, but its main job is as the small worked example used throughout the docs (every configuration's run_simple_test.sh reads the files here directly, and log_viewer/ symlinks to the reference trace produced here, rather than keeping their own copies), see validation/README.md.

docs.title: Adding an asm test
docs.text:
1. Pick an existing category folder under validation/asm/ (integer_alu/, floating_point/, control_transfer/, data_transfer/, misc/), or add a new subfolder for a new, focused group of tests.
  2. Write <name>.s. See Writing and Running Assembly Programs for the full format: the required setup, the trap table, and the pass-fail convention every test shares.
  3. Build and run it directly first, to find the actual final register values, see Assembling to generate a memory image (compiler/assemble.sh <name>.s, then model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only <name>.hex with no expected-results argument, prints the final state).
  4. Write <name>.vprj, naming <name>.s as its SOURCES and listing the register (and, if needed, memory) values from step 3 that you want checked, see the format above.
  5. Run validation/build_hex.py <folder> to (re)generate <name>.hex and <name>.objdump through the suite's own tooling (build_hex.py finds a folder's .vprj files and reads SOURCES to know what to build, so this step needs the .vprj to already exist, from step 4).
  6. Run validation/run_tests.py <folder> to check it passes.

No registration step anywhere else, run_tests.py and build_hex.py both recurse automatically.

docs.title: Adding a C test
docs.text:
1. Add a new folder under validation/C/, one per test.
  2. Write <name>.c, freestanding (no libc, see Writing and Running C Programs), following the same self-validating shape as the existing benchmarks: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed on the host, and report pass (1) or fail (0) in %o0.
  3. Write <name>.vprj, naming <name>.c as its SOURCES. Since the test already computed its own pass/fail, its RESULTS is almost always just o0=1.
  4. Run validation/build_hex.py <folder> to generate <name>.hex and <name>.objdump from it (picking compiler/compile_c.sh automatically, based on the .c extension). As with an asm test, this needs the .vprj to already exist, since build_hex.py reads its SOURCES line to know what to build.
  5. Run validation/run_tests.py <folder> to check it passes.

docs.title: Component validation suites
docs.text:
The suite above is purely functional, and purely for the SPARC core itself: every opcode, exercised in isolation or as part of a larger C program. Alongside it, dedicated test suites validate individual components, each living in its own folder:

  • validation/C/mmu/ The MMU: register access, page-table walks, TLB hit/miss/fill, faults, probe and flush, bypass. See Model Components.
  • validation/C/devices/ The timer, interrupt controller (including interrupt delivery to a real trap handler, priority, masking, and IPIs), and serial device (output, polled and interrupt-driven input). Needs core_mmu_devices. See Peripheral Devices. On the sitar_model these tests need more cycles than the default limit, so run them with --max-cycles 5000000.
  • validation/C/caches/ The L1 caches: write-through, staleness until a flush (they are not coherent), device registers never cached, atomics on a cached line. Needs core_l1cache_mmu_devices. The whole suite above also runs through the caches on that configuration, and with every ordinary access cached if you set SPARC_ALWAYS_CACHEABLE=1 in the environment.
  • validation/sparc_apara/ An APARA engine driven from a SPARC program, in five suites: basic/ (each part of the engine's interface), setup/ (bringing the engine up, and complete offloads by polling and by interrupt), threads/ (one to four engine threads), interference/ (whether threads, the SPARC and the DMA unit disturb one another), and linalg/ (linear algebra offloaded to the engine). Needs sparc_apara. On the sitar_model, run them with --max-cycles 50000000. See The Engine in a System.
  • validation/apara/ The APARA engine on its own, with its own test format and runner, in nine suites: every instruction (isa/), sequences, hazards, the branch predictor, programs the assembler must reject, timing, hand-written kernels, programs compiled from C, and the model's deviations. Unlike the SPARC suite, it also checks timing: cycle and mispredict counts, derived by hand for the default timing settings, which the timing model must match exactly. See Writing and Running APARA Programs.

For example, to run the MMU validation suite on core_mmu, build that configuration first (see Getting Started):

model/system_models/core_mmu/cpp_model/build.sh

then run the suite against it:

validation/run_tests.py validation/C/mmu --config core_mmu

This same suite runs unmodified on any other configuration that also includes an MMU, such as core_mmu_devices. Without --config, the runner uses core_only, which has no MMU, and skips the whole suite.

docs.title: Credits: validation suite of the AJIT SPARC V8 processor
docs.text:
Most of validation/asm/'s tests, and the scripts that build and run this suite, are adapted from the AJIT processor project (IIT Bombay), specifically its ajit32 instruction-level verification suite. Many more tests have since been added as part of this project (the quad-precision suite, the validation/C/ benchmarks, and the MMU suite above, none of which exist in AJIT's own tests). Tests adapted directly from AJIT carry their original author credit inline, and are listed as such in validation/asm/README.md and Authors. Tests developed as part of this project are not AJIT-derived.

A handful of specific, well-understood divergences between this model's behavior and AJIT's own reference results are documented, with side-by-side expected-vs-actual data, in docs/compliance/README.md, rather than silently patched or dropped. These are kept separate from the maintained suite (docs/compliance/, not validation/), since they represent understood implementation differences from AJIT's own hardware, not bugs in this model.

docs.title: Writing and Running Assembly Programs
docs.text:
In Getting Started, we discussed how you can view and run an existing program provided in this repository on the C++/Sitar models. A variety of asm and C test programs are present in the validation/ folder. For each program, the test source (.s or .c), the generated memory hex file, and the expected-results file are already included.

This section deals with:

  1. writing your own asm programs,
  2. assembling them to generate a memory image for the simulator,
  3. running them on the simulator, and
  4. the standard format for writing a test for inclusion in this project's validation framework.

This section assumes that you have built the models and the toolchain release. See steps 2 and 4 in Installation.

Let's create a copy of the given simple asm program test_simple_ADD, and modify it, for example, using sub instead of add.

mkdir temp_asm
cd temp_asm
cp ../validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.s test_simple_SUB.s

docs.title: Assembling to generate a memory image (.hex)
docs.text:
The conversion of asm/C programs to a memory image requires a cross-compiler toolchain, consisting of an assembler, utilities such as objdump/readelf, and also a compiler (for compiling C to asm).

If not already done in Installation (step 4), run compiler/install_toolchain.sh to create a release.

The toolchain release lives at compiler/toolchain/. Add it to your PATH variable (on Linux systems) by sourcing compiler/toolchain_env.sh, so that its binaries and libraries can be accessed from any location:

source compiler/toolchain_env.sh

Next, this project provides scripts (compiler/assemble.sh, compiler/compile_c.sh) which are convenience wrappers around these toolchain executables.

To assemble a .s to .hex:

compiler/assemble.sh <file.s>

For example, from temp_asm/:

../compiler/assemble.sh test_simple_SUB.s

This also generates test_simple_SUB.objdump, its disassembly plus full symbol table, useful for finding an address to give gdb, see Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB. See Cross Compiler for more on what's in the bundled toolchain.

docs.title: Running a test program
docs.text:
Rebuild the models with --logging, then run them on this test. From the repo root:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.hex

This prints the final register state once the program halts, see Getting Started for the full walkthrough, including the Sitar-timed model (which takes the identical CLI) and observing the trace in the log viewer.

docs.title: Creating a test
docs.text:
A test is not just any program that runs on a model, but one that gives a pass/fail indication after checking something. In this project, a test consists of a source file and an expected-results file in a specific format, see "Recommended format for a test program" below for how the source file itself needs to be structured to make this possible.

The simulator executables take the following arguments:

sparc_sim_cpp_core_only <hex_file> [expected_results_file] [max_cycles]
  • A hex file (required): the memory image to run.
  • An expected-results file (optional): if given, once the program halts, the final state is checked against it, and the executable prints a PASS/FAIL verdict per check plus an OVERALL result, instead of the detailed state.
  • A cycle limit (optional): caps how long the simulator runs before giving up.

When no expected-results file is passed, as above, the executable just prints the final register state. When one is passed, it's checked directly instead.

Let's write an expected-results file for our test, and run with that. o0 = 5 - 7 = 0xfffffffe, so temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.expected:

REG o0 0xfffffffe

Then run it:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.hex temp_asm/test_simple_SUB.expected

docs.title: Format for the expected-results file
docs.text:
test_simple_SUB.expected is a plain text file, one check per line:

  • REG <name> <hex value> [mask] checks a register (mnemonics g1-g7, o0-o7, l0-l7, i0-i7, f0-f31, psr, fpsr, y, wim, tbr, pc, npc, asr0-asr31).
  • MEM <hex addr> <hex value> [mask] checks a word-aligned 32-bit memory read.

Either kind accepts an optional trailing mask, to check only specific bits.

docs.title: Recommended format for a test program
docs.text:
Because this model does not yet have any operating system, the test program has to be self-sufficient. This means initializing the processor state, setting up a trap table, then running the test part and exiting while indicating pass/fail in some way to the simulator. In the current scheme, the latter is achieved using %g1 as a sentinel register together with a deliberate final trap (ta 0), described in full under "The pass-fail convention" below.

The following shows a typical structure of a test program:

.global main
main:
_start:
    ! 1. Enable traps: PSR ET=1, PS=1, S=1
    mov 0xE0, %l0
    wr %l0, %psr
    nop
    nop
    nop

    ! 2. Point TBR at this file's own trap table
    set trap_table_base, %l0
    wr %l0, 0x0, %tbr
    nop
    nop
    nop

    ! 3. Sentinel: overwritten by the trap number if anything unexpected traps
    mov 0xBAD, %g1

    !======================================
    ! 4. The instruction(s) under test go here
    add %o0, %o1, %o2
    !======================================

    ta 0            ! 5. normal exit
    nop
    nop

not_reached:
    set 0xDEAD, %g1 ! control should never reach here
    ta 0
    nop
    nop

    .align 4096     ! TBR only captures bits 31:12, so the trap table
                     ! must start on a 4096-byte boundary
trap_table_base:
    ! 256 four-instruction slots, one per trap type (0x00-0xff):
    !   mov <trap number>, %g1 ; restore ; ta 0 ; nop
    ! ... (copy this verbatim from any existing test, see below)

Our own test_simple_SUB skips the trap table by simply disabling traps entirely (wr %g0, %psr), the simplest thing that works when nothing in the test could ever trap. Use the fuller structure above instead for anything meant to join validation/asm/, where an unexpected trap needs to be caught rather than silently forcing error_mode for the wrong reason.

Copy the trap table, don't retype it

The 256-entry trap table is always the same boilerplate. Copy it verbatim from any existing test under validation/asm/, then edit only the one slot you actually care about, see "The trap table" below.

docs.title: The pass-fail convention
docs.text:
Every test always halts the same way: a ta 0 taken with traps disabled (ET=0, cleared automatically on trap entry) forces the processor into error_mode per the manual (Appendix C, Section C.8). This is what PROCESSOR STATE: ERROR in sparc_sim_cpp's output means, and it's expected, not a bug.

%g1 distinguishes a clean run from an unexpected trap:

  • If the test's own final ta 0 (step 5 above) is what triggers this, its trap-table slot (SW_trap_0x80) sets %g1 = 0x80. This is success: nothing unexpected happened.
  • If any other trap occurs first (a bug, a mistake in the test, or a trap you're deliberately testing for), it's caught by that trap's own table slot, which records the trap number into %g1 before re-trapping the same way. So %g1's final value tells you exactly what happened, whether the test passed or not.

docs.title: The trap table
docs.text: Each slot is a fixed 4 instructions: mov <tt>, %g1; restore; ta 0; nop. To make a test verify a specific trap actually fires (rather than just detecting an unexpected one), replace that one slot with custom code. For example, validation/asm/floating_point/fp_exceptions/overflow.s replaces its HW_trap_0x08 slot with inc %g2; rett %r18; nop; nop, which increments a counter and resumes execution right after the trapping instruction (via rett), instead of halting. This lets the test both confirm the trap fired (%g2) and continue on to a normal exit (%g1 = 0x80).

docs.title: Adding it to the validation suite
docs.text:
Hand-writing a .expected file and running it yourself works for one test at a time. To run your test alongside the rest of the suite automatically instead, and have it re-checked every time the model changes, the recommended practice is to wrap it as a .vprj file for use with the validation script. See Validation Suite: Adding an asm test for details.

See validation/asm/README.md for the AJIT-adaptation attribution and docs/compliance/README.md for documented, specific divergences from AJIT's own reference results (kept separate from the maintained suite since they represent understood implementation differences, not bugs).

docs.title: Writing and Running C Programs
docs.text: Hand-assembling an algorithm like a sort or an FFT one instruction at a time, the way validation/asm/'s tests do, is tedious once the program is more than a handful of instructions long (see Validation Suite). validation/C/ takes the other approach: write the test as ordinary, freestanding C, compile it with the bundled cross-toolchain, and run it the same way. This page covers writing one, building and running it, and checking its result.

docs.title: No standard library, by design
docs.text:
This model has no operating system. There is nothing for a C standard library to call into. printf has no console to write to. malloc has no OS to request pages from. C programs for this model must be freestanding: no #include <stdio.h>, no libc at all, just the C language itself plus whatever you implement by hand against the flat memory space MemCore provides.

In the configurations with devices (core_mmu_devices and up), the Serial Device is the console: a program writes characters to it, and the simulator prints them. See Using the peripheral devices below.

docs.title: Structuring a test program
docs.text:
Write an ordinary, freestanding C main(). Every test in validation/C/ follows the same self-validating shape: compute something, compare it against a golden value computed once on the host machine and hardcoded right there in the source, and report pass(1)/ fail(0) in %o0. Here's a real one in full, validation/C/array_sum/array_sum.c, summing a small array:

// array_sum.c
//
// A first bare-metal C validation test, and the template every other
// validation/C/ test follows: sums the elements of a small integer array
// in a loop, then checks the result against a golden value computed once
// on the host machine (here, by hand: 1+2+3+4+5=15) and hardcoded below.
// Self-validating this way means the .vprj only ever has to check one
// thing -- that %o0 is 1 -- rather than re-embedding (and risking a
// second, independent typo in) the actual expected sum.
//
// See docs/writing_and_running_c_programs.md and compiler/crt0.s for how
// this gets a working stack, trap table, and pass/fail halt convention,
// the same way every validation/asm/ test does.

int main(void)
{
    int values[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    int sum = 0;
    int i;
    int expected;
    int pass;

    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++)
        sum += values[i];

    expected = 15; // 1+2+3+4+5, computed on the host
    pass = (sum == expected) ? 1 : 0;

    // Report pass(1)/fail(0) in %o0 -- see the file comment above.
    __asm__ volatile ("mov %0, %%o0" : : "r" (pass));

    // Halt: traps are enabled (crt0.s), so this ta 0 is caught by its
    // trap-table slot, which re-traps with traps now disabled, forcing
    // the model into error_mode. That's this project's pass/fail halt
    // convention, see writing_and_running_assembly_programs.md.
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");

    // Never reached: ta 0 above always halts the simulation first. This
    // just satisfies the compiler, which otherwise warns that a
    // non-void main() falls off the end without returning a value.
    while (1) {}
    return 0;
}

main() must never return, since there's nothing to return into. The way to end a test is the same mechanism validation/asm/ tests use, described in full in Writing and Running Assembly Programs: a single line of inline assembly, __asm__ volatile ("ta 0"), at the end of main().

Unlike an assembly test, you don't write any of the surrounding setup by hand. compiler/crt0.s is linked ahead of your compiled .c file (entry point overridden to crt0.s's own _start) and does it for you:

  • enables traps and installs the same 256-entry trap table every validation/asm/ test installs,
  • sets up a working stack (needed for any C function using a local variable, which %sp starting at 0 does not provide on its own),
  • initializes %g1 as the pass/fail sentinel,
  • then calls your main().

It leaves the FPU off (the PSR's EF bit clear), so a program that computes with float or double sets EF itself first, or its first floating-point instruction traps. validation/sparc_apara/apara_common.h has a small enable_fpu() that does this.

Here's what that looks like once linked, array_sum's actual entry point, before main even runs:

00000000 <_start>:
       0:   01 00 00 00     nop
       4:   01 00 00 00     nop
       8:   a0 10 20 e0     mov  0xe0, %l0  ! e0 <not_reached+0x98>
       c:   81 8c 00 00     mov  %l0, %psr
      10:   01 00 00 00     nop
      14:   01 00 00 00     nop
      18:   01 00 00 00     nop
      1c:   21 00 00 04     sethi  %hi(0x1000), %l0
      20:   a0 14 20 00     mov  %l0, %l0   ! 1000 <HW_trap_0x00>
      24:   81 9c 20 00     mov  %l0, %tbr
      28:   01 00 00 00     nop
      2c:   01 00 00 00     nop
      30:   01 00 00 00     nop
      34:   1d 03 ff ff     sethi  %hi(0xffffc00), %sp
      38:   9c 13 a3 f0     or  %sp, 0x3f0, %sp ! ffffff0 <memcpy+0xfffdf48>
      3c:   82 10 2b ad     mov  0xbad, %g1
      40:   40 00 07 f0     call  2000 <main>
      44:   01 00 00 00     nop

Matching it up against the four steps above: the mov 0xe0,%l0/wr %l0,%psr pair enables traps (see Writing and Running Assembly Programs for the 0xE0 encoding), sethi/wr ...,%tbr points TBR at the trap table linked in right after it (HW_trap_0x00 onward, the annotation on that line), sethi/or ...,%sp sets up the stack, mov 0xbad,%g1 is the sentinel, and the final call main (with its delay-slot nop) is the handoff into your code. See crt0.s itself for the full explanation of each step.

The result is that a C test's ta 0 halts exactly the same way an assembly test's does, and an unexpected trap during your test is caught the same way too.

Checking the result is then a single line. Its .vprj only ever has to check that %o0 is 1:

SOURCES = array_sum.c

RESULTS =
o0=1

The alternative: checking memory directly

Writing a raw computed value to a global and checking it directly via a .vprj MEM line (the address found in the .objdump's symbol table, or readelf -s array_sum.elf directly) still works. It's the same REG/MEM format validation/asm/ uses, but means the golden value is embedded in two places (the .vprj and, since the test already computes its own pass/fail, the source) instead of one. Doing the comparison in C and reporting a single pass/fail flag avoids that, and doubles as a self-contained mini-benchmark that also happens to check itself. See the rest of validation/C/ for more worked examples.

docs.title: Building and running it
docs.text:
A minimal, freestanding C compiler (GCC 4.4.3) is bundled alongside the existing sparc-elf assembler, linker, readelf, and objdump, installed together by Installation step 4, if you haven't already. See Cross Compiler for what's bundled and why, and for building your own, more modern cross-toolchain instead.

compiler/compile_c.sh your_program.c

This produces your_program.hex, the same kind of memory image compiler/assemble.sh produces for assembly tests, loadable the same way. It also produces your_program.objdump: a readable disassembly of the linked program (useful for seeing what the compiler actually generated, unlike a hand-written .s file, this isn't something you wrote directly), followed by the full symbol table, function and global-variable addresses included. See Examining Core State at Runtime Using GDB.

Run it directly against the model the same way as an assembly test, see Running a test program:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only your_program.hex

docs.title: Using the peripheral devices
docs.text:
compiler/include/ holds header-only routines for the devices. compile_c.sh puts that folder on the include path.

Header Provides device_addresses.h Every device register address (ADDR_TIMER_CONTROL_REGISTER, ...) and interrupt level (TIMER_IRL, ...). ajit_access_routines.h Physical (MMU-bypass) loads and stores, ajit_get_core_and_thread_id(), and the Timer and Serial routines, e.g. __ajit_serial_putchar_via_bypass__(), __ajit_serial_getchar_via_bypass__(), __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__(). ajit_mt_irc.h Interrupt Controller routines (enableInterruptController(), writeInterruptControlRegister(), ...) and interrupt dispatch (ajit_set_interrupt_handler()). ajit_ipi.h Inter-processor interrupts (__ajit_set_ipi_interrupt__(), ...). apara_access_routines.h The APARA engine, in sparc_apara: loading its program, starting its threads, its DMA unit (apara_load_program(), apara_start_thread(), ...). See The Engine in a System. stdint.h uint32_t and friends, which the bundled compiler does not provide on its own.

Printing a message:

#include "ajit_access_routines.h"

int main(void)
{
    char message[] = "Hello from SPARC\n";
    __ajit_serial_configure_via_bypass__(1, 0, 0);   //enable the transmitter
    __ajit_serial_puts_via_bypass__(message, sizeof(message) - 1);
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");
    while (1) {}
}

docs.title: Taking interrupts
docs.text:
The default startup code, crt0.s, halts on every trap other than the final ta 0. A program that takes interrupts links compiler/crt0_interrupts.s instead, which also handles register window overflow and underflow, and sends every interrupt to ajit_generic_interrupt_handler() (in ajit_mt_irc.h). That function disables the thread's Interrupt Controller slot, calls the handler registered for the interrupt's level, and enables the slot again (the sequence on the Interrupt Controller page). The handler itself only has to clear its source:

#include "ajit_access_routines.h"
#include "ajit_mt_irc.h"

volatile int ticks = 0;

void timer_handler(void)
{
    ticks++;
    __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__(0);   //clear the source
}

int main(void)
{
    ajit_initialize_interrupt_handlers_to_null();
    ajit_set_interrupt_handler(TIMER_IRL, timer_handler);
    writeInterruptControlRegister(0, 0, (1 << TIMER_IRL) | 1);   //slot 0: enable, timer level
    __ajit_write_timer_control_register_via_bypass__((1000 << 1) | 1);
    while (ticks == 0) {}
    __asm__ volatile ("ta 0");
    while (1) {}
}

Select the interrupt startup code with a STARTUP line in the test's .vprj (see below), or with CRT0=crt0_interrupts.s compile_c.sh ... on the command line. Handlers run with traps enabled but every maskable interrupt masked, so they do not nest.

docs.title: Adding it to the validation suite
docs.text: Same two-phase pipeline as validation/asm/, see Validation Suite. build_hex.py picks compiler/assemble.sh or compiler/compile_c.sh automatically, based on whether a test's SOURCES line names a .s or a .c file. See Validation Suite: Adding a C test for the exact steps.

docs.title: The APARA Engine
docs.text:
APARA is a compute engine designed to sit next to a SPARC processor as an accelerator. It is built for vector work on small integers and low-precision floats (dot products, reductions, element-wise arithmetic on 4- to 64-bit elements), the kind of computation that is slow on a general-purpose core but very regular. The SPARC processor loads the engine's programs, starts its threads, and moves data in and out of it, while the engine does the number crunching.

The engine was designed at IIT Bombay (Prof. Madhav Desai). This project models it in the same two ways as the SPARC core: a fast functional model, and a Sitar timing model of its pipeline.

docs.title: The engine at a glance
docs.text:
• Bundles The engine is a VLIW machine. Instead of one instruction at a time, it executes bundles of up to 8 instructions, which the program has grouped to run together.
  • Four hardware threads Each thread has its own 32 64-bit registers and its own PC, and the four share one five-stage pipeline. When one thread waits, for a result or a branch, the others keep the pipeline busy.
  • A type in every instruction A register is just 64 bits. Each instruction says how to read it: as one 64-bit integer, as 8 $i8 elements, as 16 $f4 floats, and so on. One vector instruction thus does up to 16 operations.
  • Local memories 16 KB of instruction memory (IMEM) and 64 KB of data memory (DMEM), in two banks, close to the pipeline and fast. In a system, the engine reaches main memory too, more slowly, and its DMA unit copies data in and out.

docs.title: In this project
docs.text:
Two configurations model the engine:

  • apara One engine on its own. A program and its data are placed in the engine's memories before the run. This is the place to write and test engine programs, and to study the engine's timing.
  • sparc_apara A SPARC core (with L1 caches, MMU, and peripheral devices) and one engine. The SPARC program loads and runs the engine's programs, and both the engine's DMA unit and its own loads and stores reach the system's memory.

Both come with functional and timing models, tests, and tools.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• To write and run engine programs, read the Instruction Set, then Assembly Language and Tools, then Writing and Running Programs.
  • To write engine programs in C, such as linear algebra kernels, read The C Compiler.
  • To use the engine from a SPARC program, read The Engine in a System.
  • To study or change the engine's timing, read the Timing Model.
  • For the model's sources, where it deliberately departs from them, and the open questions (mainly for the model's authors), see Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: The code
docs.text: Where What model/cpp_common_code/apara/ The engine in plain C++, shared by both models: its state and execution (AparaCore), instruction decoding and arithmetic, the file formats and command line, and, for sparc_apara, the control unit, the DMA unit, and the three joined together for the cpp_model. Also the timing model's latency table and pipeline helpers (AparaTiming.h). model/sitar_component_models/Apara*.sitar The timing model: AparaEngine and its five stage modules, and AparaHost, the engine's host side in sparc_apara. model/sitar_component_models/SystemInterconnect.sitar sparc_apara's two-master bus. model/system_models/apara/, model/system_models/sparc_apara/ The two configurations, each with its cpp_model/ and sitar_model/. compiler/apara/ The assembler, the disassembler, the C compiler (apcc.py, with include/apara.h), the program-to-C-header tool, and vim syntax highlighting. compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h The SPARC-side C routines. validation/apara/ The engine's own test suites, and their runner (see Tests). validation/sparc_apara/ The tests of the SPARC using the engine (see Tests).

docs.title: APARA Assembly Language and Tools
docs.text:
APARA programs are written in mcode, the engine's assembly language, and assembled with this project's own tools in compiler/apara/. (They can also be written in a subset of C, see The C Compiler, which writes mcode for these tools.) The tools are plain Python 3, using only the standard library, so there is nothing to install.

The assembler checks programs strictly: it stops with an error on anything it cannot encode exactly, rather than producing a wrong program (see Error messages).

docs.title: A first program
docs.text:
// Sum the 8-bit elements of a vector in $r1, store the result.

sum:
    ||
        $vreduce + $r2 ($vi8) $r1       // 1+2+...+8 = 36
    ;
store:
    ||
        $st ($i64) [$r0 + 16] $r2       // DMEM bytes 16..23
    ;
    || $halt ;

The program's three bundles run one after another:

  1. $vreduce reads $r1 as a vector of eight 8-bit signed elements and adds them up, into $r2.
  2. $st stores $r2, as a 64-bit integer, at DMEM address $r0 + 16, that is, 16 ($r0 is always 0).
  3. $halt stops the thread.

$r1 is set before the run: by a registers file given to the simulator (see File formats), or, in a test, by the INIT section of its .vprj (see Writing and Running Programs).

docs.title: Program structure
docs.text:
• Bundles A program is a sequence of bundles. Each starts with ||, holds one to eight instructions, and ends with ;. A bundle may be written on one line or span several.
  • Labels A bundle may have a label (sum:), which branches and calls can name as their target.
  • Comments // starts a comment, to the end of the line.
  • Instructions Every instruction is listed in APARA Instruction Set.

docs.title: What the assembler does
docs.text:
Beyond translating each instruction, the assembler turns the bundles as written into bundles the engine can run. It does this in seven steps:

  1. Parses and checks every instruction: register numbers, types, immediate and increment ranges, and whether each operation is allowed for its type.
  2. Checks each bundle: at most 8 instructions, at most one branch/call/return, at most 4 loads and stores, at most one divide or square root, and no register written by two instructions.
  3. Closes each bundle, filling it with $nulls up to its size: 8 slots if it holds a control transfer, load or store, divide, or square root, otherwise the smallest power of two that fits.
  4. Places the bundles in IMEM, each at an address that is a multiple of its size, filling any gaps with $null bundles.
  5. Arranges the slots of each 8-slot bundle: the control transfer in slot 0, a divide or square root in slot 1, loads and stores in slots 4 to 7, and the other instructions, in source order, in the free slots.
  6. Resolves labels: a branch or call holds its target relative to its own address (its bundle's address plus its slot).
  7. Encodes every instruction, setting bit 31 on each bundle's first word.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode                 # writes prog.obj
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode -o out.obj \
        --aligned prog.aligned.mcode --listing prog.lst
python3 compiler/apara/apara_dis.py prog.obj                  # mcode, to standard output
  • apara_as.py, the assembler. It writes an object file, by default named after the source. Two options write more:
    • --aligned writes the program as placed and arranged, every bundle with its address: the program the engine actually runs.
    • --listing writes each word's address, encoding, and instruction.
  • apara_dis.py, the disassembler. It turns an object file back into mcode, naming branch and call targets L_<address>. Its output assembles back to the same object file.
  • apara_obj_to_c.py, for programs the SPARC loads into the engine (in sparc_apara). It writes an engine program, in mcode or in C, as a C header, containing the program as an array and each label's address as a #define. See The Engine in a System.
  • apcc.py, the C compiler, see The C Compiler.

python3 compiler/apara/test_mcode.py runs the assembler's and disassembler's own unit tests. The assembler's checks are also tested by the validation/apara/asm_errors/ suite: programs it must reject.

docs.title: Error messages
docs.text:
Any error stops the assembly, with the file, the line, and the reason:

prog.mcode:12: error: $r2 is written twice in this bundle (also at line 11)

Some messages, and what they mean:

Message Cause immediate 600 is out of range (-512 to 511) Immediates are 10-bit signed. a bundle holds at most one divide or square root The engine has one divider, shared by divides and square roots. floats have only + - * / No logic operations or shifts on float types. the registers from $r30 run past $r31 A $u256 transfer needs 4 consecutive registers. a vector cast changes the element width by one step ($vi8) to ($vi32) needs two casts. undefined label x A misspelled label.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
The tools and the simulators share these file formats. In every format, numbers are hexadecimal and ! starts a comment.

File Lines Example object (.obj) <word index>: <instruction word> 8: 80000000 data (data.map) <dword index>: <64-bit value> 10: 0x0102030405060708 registers <thread> <register> <value> 0 1f 0x10 results <thread> pc <pc> [mask] 0 pc 0x21 <thread> reg <register> <value> [mask] 0 reg 0x5 0x67 <thread> mem <dword index> <value> [mask] 0 mem 0x4 0x00aa000000001234 <thread> error <ERROR> [mask] (this project's addition) 0 error 0x2000000

A data file gives DMEM's initial contents by dword (8-byte word) index, taken modulo the DMEM size: index 0x10 is DMEM bytes 0x80 to 0x87. A results file lists the expected final state, and a mask, if given, selects the bits compared.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text:
• vim: compiler/apara/vim/mcode.vim. Copy it to ~/.vim/syntax/, and add au BufRead,BufNewFile *.mcode set filetype=mcode to ~/.vimrc.
  • This documentation highlights ```mcode code blocks with the Pygments lexer in docs/mcode_pygments_lexer/.

docs.title: The APARA C Compiler
docs.text:
compiler/apara/apcc.py compiles a small subset of C to mcode, the engine's assembly language. It lets you write engine programs, such as linear algebra kernels, in a familiar language, and still reach the engine's vector instructions where they matter.

It is a teaching compiler, kept small enough to read: one Python file, standard library only. It does not optimize much, and it leaves out the parts of C that need a stack, since the engine has none. Its output is plain mcode, so you can read what it produced, and replace a part with hand-written mcode when speed matters (see inline mcode).

The tool chain, for a program prog.c:

prog.c --apcc.py--> prog.mcode --apara_as.py--> prog.obj --> simulator
               \--> prog.data  (DMEM's initial contents) --> simulator

docs.title: A first program
docs.text:
A dot product of two 64-element int8_t vectors, from validation/apara/c_programs/dot_vector.c:

#define N 64
int8_t A[N] = {-43, -9, 13, 117, ...};
int8_t B[N] = {54, -114, -11, -113, ...};
int64_t result;

void main(void)
{
    int64_t sum = 0;
    for (int64_t i = 0; i < N; i += 8)
        sum = __dot_acc("vi8", sum, __ld64(&A[i]), __ld64(&B[i]));
    result = sum;
}

The global arrays live in DMEM. Each __ld64 loads 8 elements as one 64-bit value, and __dot_acc multiplies the 8 pairs and adds the products to sum, in one $dot instruction. Compile, assemble, and run it on the standalone engine:

python3 compiler/apara/apcc.py dot_vector.c        # writes dot_vector.mcode and dot_vector.data
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py dot_vector.mcode
model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/executable/apara_sim_cpp \
        -i dot_vector.obj -d dot_vector.data --dump-results -

! thread 0 halted, ERROR 0x2000000
0 pc 0x48
0 mem 0x10 0xffffffffffff248c
...

result is DMEM dword 0x10 (byte address 0x80), and holds -56180. The compiler lists where it put each global at the top of the mcode file:

// DMEM layout (byte offsets):
//   A                0x0000  int8_t[64]
//   B                0x0040  int8_t[64]
//   result           0x0080  int64_t
// Generated by apcc.py (-O1). Edit the C source, not this file.

main:
    || + $r1 ($i64) $r0 0  + $r2 ($i64) $r0 0 ;
    || - $r3 ($i64) $r2 64 ;
    || ? ($i64) $r3 >= $goto L3_done ;
L1_loop:
    ...
    || $ld ($i64) $r4 [$r5 + 0] ;
    || $dot $accumulate $r1 ($vi8) $r3 $r4 ;
L2_next:
    || + $r2 ($i64) $r2 8 ;
    || - $r3 ($i64) $r2 64 ;
    || ? ($i64) $r3 < $goto L1_loop ;
L3_done:
    || $st ($i64) [$r0 + 128] $r1  $halt ;

Comments in the mcode give the C line each part came from.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
python3 compiler/apara/apcc.py prog.c [-o prog.mcode] [--data prog.data] \
        [--symbols prog.sym] [-O0] [--dmem-base addr]
Option Does -o <file> The mcode file (default: the source's name with .mcode). --data <file> DMEM's initial contents, a data file (default: .data), from the globals' initializers. --symbols <file> Also write each global's DMEM byte offset, one name offset per line. -O0 One instruction per bundle. The default, -O1, packs independent instructions into bundles (see Code generation). --dmem-base <addr> The address of DMEM byte 0 as the program sees it: 0 (the default) for the standalone engine, 0x01000000 for the engine in sparc_apara, whose DMEM is a window in the system's address space (see In a system).

Errors stop the compilation, with the file, the line, and the reason:

apcc.py: error: prog.c:2: recursion (f -> f) is not supported
apcc.py: error: prog.c:7: x is not defined

python3 compiler/apara/test_apcc.py runs the compiler's own unit tests: small programs whose layout, output and error messages it checks, and whose mcode must assemble. The programs' results are checked by the validation/apara/c_programs/ suite.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
C type Engine type int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t (and char, short, int, long) $i8 .. $i64 uint8_t .. uint64_t (and unsigned char ..) $u8 .. $u64 float, double $f32, $f64 void (functions only)

Integer expressions are computed in 64 bits (unsigned if an operand is uint64_t, signed otherwise), much as C widens small types before arithmetic. A value is wrapped to its type's width when it is stored in a narrower variable or array element, or cast to a narrower type. Float expressions are computed in float, or in double if an operand is a double. A cast converts explicitly ((int32_t) x, (double) i).

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
• Global variables, scalars and one- or two-dimensional arrays, live in DMEM. They are laid out from address 0 in declaration order, each aligned to 8 bytes, unless __at(addr) places one at a fixed DMEM byte address (a multiple of 8):

    int8_t A[64] __at(0x100);

    They may have constant initializers, which go into the data file. Without one, a global starts as zero on the standalone engine, whose DMEM starts as zero (in a system, see In a system).

  • Local variables and parameters are scalars, each kept in a register for the function's whole life. There is no stack, so there are no local arrays.

docs.title: Statements and expressions
docs.text:
• Statements: declarations, assignments (=, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=), ++ and --, if and else, while, do ... while, for, break, continue, return, and blocks.
  • Expressions: the usual arithmetic, bitwise, shift, comparison and logical operators, ?:, casts, array indexing (A[i], M[i][j]), &A[i] (an element's DMEM byte address, for the intrinsics), and calls.
  • Preprocessor: object-like #define NAME value. Other preprocessor lines, #include among them, are ignored.

docs.title: Functions and threads
docs.text:
• Functions may call other functions, but not recursively (directly or through others). Each variable gets its own register, different from those of every function on a call chain through it, so a call has nothing to save: it is a $call and a $return.
  • __entry marks a thread's entry point. Its parameters arrive in $r1, $r2, ... (set before the thread starts), and returning from it halts the thread. A program may have several entry points, one per kind of thread. Without any __entry, main is the entry point.

Several threads may run the same entry function, each with its own arguments. From c_programs/matmul_threads.c, a matrix product whose rows are split among threads:

__entry void rows(int64_t first, int64_t count)
{
    for (int64_t i = first; i < first + count; i++)
        for (int64_t j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            int64_t sum = 0;
            for (int64_t k = 0; k < N; k++)
                sum += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
            C[i][j] = sum;
        }
}

Every thread has its own registers, so each has its own i, j, k and sum. They share the global arrays, so each must write only its own part of them: the engine has no atomic operations (see Threads sharing data).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The limits, by design:

  • No recursion, no pointers (other than integer DMEM addresses), no structs, no local arrays.
  • At most about 28 variables live along any call chain (the engine has 31 usable registers, and expressions need temporaries). The compiler says so when a program needs more.
  • Comparisons test the sign of the difference, so two 64-bit operands must differ by less than 263.
  • No standard library. There is nowhere to print to: a program leaves its results in DMEM.

docs.title: Intrinsics
docs.text:
The intrinsics reach the vector instructions. Each works on 64-bit values holding packed vectors, as the engine's registers do. T names the element type, as a string: "vi8", "vu16", "vf32", and so on (vi, vu or vf, 4 to 32 bits).

Intrinsic Instruction Does __ld64(addr), __st64(addr, v) $ld, $st ($i64) A 64-bit load or store at a DMEM byte address (&A[i]): 8 int8_t elements at once, for example. __dot(T, a, b) $dot The sum of the element products. __dot_acc(T, acc, a, b) $dot $accumulate acc + __dot(T, a, b). __vadd, __vsub, __vmul (T, a, b) $v + - * Element-wise. __vadd_rep, __vsub_rep, __vmul_rep (T, a, s) $v ... $replicate The same, with s's lowest element for every element of the second operand. __vreduce(OP, T, a) $vreduce All the elements combined by OP: "+", "*", "|", "&", "^". __fsqrt(x) $fsqrt The square root of a float or double. __slice(x, high, low) $slice Bits [high:low] of x (constant positions). __halt() $halt Stop the thread here.

docs.title: Inline mcode
docs.text:
__asm__("...") puts mcode into the program as it is, with %name standing for a variable's register. One instruction becomes a bundle of its own; a whole bundle, || ... ;, is kept as written. The compiler never moves other instructions into, or across, inline mcode. From c_programs/inline_asm.c:

int64_t v = 0x0102030405060708;
int64_t s = 0;
int64_t t = 0;
__asm__("$vreduce + %s ($vi8) %v");                       // s = 36
__asm__("|| + %t ($i64) %s %s  - %v ($i64) %v %v ;");   // t = 72, v = 0

The second bundle shows the engine's bundle semantics: both instructions read s and v as they were before the bundle.

docs.title: Checking a program on the host
docs.text:
compiler/apara/include/apara.h defines __entry, __at and every intrinsic in plain C, so the same program also compiles with an ordinary C compiler, to check its results on the host before running it on the engine. A small harness calls the program and prints its results:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "apara.h"
#define main kernel_main
#include "dot_vector.c"
#undef main

int main(void)
{
    kernel_main();
    printf("result = %lld\n", (long long) result);   // -56180, as on the engine
    return 0;
}

gcc -I compiler/apara/include host_check.c -o host_check && ./host_check

apcc.py ignores the #include, and knows the intrinsics itself. On the host, __ld64 and __st64 use the host's byte order. Element-wise results and dot products come out the same as on the engine, but the elements' positions within a 64-bit value differ, so __slice of a loaded vector does not.

docs.title: Code generation
docs.text:
• One register per variable, temporaries for expressions.
  • Loops test at the bottom, so each iteration takes one branch, which the branch predictor learns (see Branch prediction).
  • Bundles. With -O1, a scheduler packs consecutive instructions into one bundle when none depends on another, and when the bundle stays legal (at most one control transfer, four memory operations and one divide, and no register written twice). Since every instruction in a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle, the result is the same as running the instructions one by one. -O0 puts every instruction in its own bundle, for comparison: the c_programs/dot_scalar and dot_scalar_O0 tests run the same program both ways.

The hardware resolves every dependence between bundles (see Hazards), so the compiler never needs to insert waits: a bundle that needs an earlier result waits in the pipeline until it is ready. The compiler's job, for speed, is to give the pipeline independent work, by unrolling loops by hand, or by splitting the work among threads.

docs.title: Linear algebra on the engine
docs.text:
The engine's strength is packed vectors of small elements: one $dot on $vi8 operands is 8 multiplications and 8 additions. A linear algebra kernel gets that speed when its inner loop works on whole 64-bit words.

  • Dot products and matrix products: load 8 int8_t (or 4 int16_t) elements with __ld64, and accumulate with __dot_acc, as in the first program. For a matrix product, store the second matrix transposed, so that a column is contiguous in DMEM.
  • Element-wise operations (vector addition, scaling): __vadd, __vmul_rep (a vector times a scalar), and __st64 to store 8 results at once (c_programs/vadd_vector.c).
  • Floating point: float and double arithmetic compiles to the engine's float instructions (c_programs/saxpy.c: y = a·x + y).
  • More threads: give each thread its own rows or its own slice, as matmul_threads.c does, and start every thread at the entry function, each with its own arguments.

The test folder validation/apara/c_programs/ has each of these, with expected results computed independently. Running one is the quickest way to start (see Writing and Running Programs). For example, matmul_threads.c on three threads, on the timing model, reports its cycles and how the pipeline spent them:

python3 compiler/apara/apcc.py matmul_threads.c
python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py matmul_threads.mcode
printf '0 1 0x0\n0 2 0x2\n1 1 0x2\n1 2 0x2\n2 1 0x4\n2 2 0x2\n' > registers.txt   # first row, row count
model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/executable/apara_sim_sitar -p 0x0 -p 0x0 -p 0x0 \
        -i matmul_threads.obj -d matmul_threads.data -a registers.txt --stats

ran 4554 bundles in 7125 cycles
...
register-lock stalls     914 cycles
REGFILE token stalls     1670 cycles

rows is at IMEM address 0x0 here, so each -p 0x0 starts one more thread there (apara_as.py --aligned shows every label's address). Each thread gets two rows, through $r1 and $r2. The counters show where the time goes: APARA Timing Model explains them.

docs.title: In a system
docs.text:
In sparc_apara, a SPARC program loads the engine program and its data, starts its threads, and collects the results. The engine's DMEM appears there as a window at 0x0100_0000, and an engine program must address it that way (any other address goes out to the system's main memory). So a C kernel for the system is compiled with --dmem-base 0x01000000.

compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py does that, and turns the result into a C header for the SPARC program:

python3 compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py vector_stats.c     # writes vector_stats.c.h

static const uint32_t vector_stats_program[] = { ... };   // the IMEM words
#define VECTOR_STATS_PROGRAM_WORDS 160
#define VECTOR_STATS_MAIN 0x0                               // each function's IMEM address
#define VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_DATA 0x0                          // each global's DMEM byte offset
#define VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_SUM 0x100
...
static const uint32_t vector_stats_dmem_image[] = { ... };  // the initializers
#define VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS 0

kernel_dmem_image[] holds only the non-zero words of the initial data. DMEM is zero at power-up, but keeps whatever an earlier program left there, so a kernel that is run after another one should not count on its uninitialized (or zero-initialized) globals being zero: the SPARC program clears them, or the kernel sets them itself.

The SPARC program then uses the engine through the routines of compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h:

#include "vector_stats.c.h"

apara_load_program(vector_stats_program, VECTOR_STATS_PROGRAM_WORDS);
apara_load_dmem_image(vector_stats_dmem_image, VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS);
apara_dma_load(0, VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_DATA, (uint32_t) data, sizeof(data));   // the input
apara_start_thread(0, VECTOR_STATS_MAIN);
apara_wait_thread(0);
sum = apara_dmem_read_dword(VECTOR_STATS_DMEM_SUM);                       // the result

The Engine in a System describes these steps in full. A test in the validation suite names its C kernels in its .vprj, with an MCODE = vector_stats.c line, and validation/build_hex.py writes the header before compiling the test.

docs.title: APARA: Deviations and Findings
docs.text:
This project's APARA model is its own implementation of the engine, written from the engine's documents and checked against APARA's reference model. Its sources, in order of authority:

  1. The microarchitecture document (APARA Engine: Microarchitecture and Timing, engine_isp/docs/microarch in the APARA repository), for the engine's structure and timing. Its latency table gives the timing model's default latencies. The timing model has been checked against this document, but not yet against the hardware's own (Aa_model) simulation traces.
  2. The ISA document (engine_isp/isa/isa.txt in the APARA repository), for what each instruction does.
  3. The reference model, McodeMachine, with its tools (mcode_align, mcode_assemble, mcode_run). The narrow-float conversion rules (see Instruction Set) are exactly its rules. Its alignment (mcode_align) and assembly (mcode_assemble) steps are one step in this project's assembler, which uses the same file formats, so files move freely between the two sets of tools; the simulators accept mcode_run's options.

For every program the reference tools handle correctly, the model gives the same results: the assembler writes the same object file, and a run reaches the same final state (PC, registers, DMEM). This was checked on every valid program of the APARA repository, and on this project's own tests (see Writing and Running Programs).

This page lists where the model deliberately differs from the reference model, and why, followed by the open questions in the sources, which are to be reviewed with APARA's designers. Every test that depends on a deviation has a DEVIATION line in its .vprj, and the tests of the deviations themselves are collected in validation/apara/deviations/.

docs.title: Deviations from the reference model
docs.text: Each row gives what the reference model does, what this model does instead, and why. Most are fixes of defects in the reference model, where it contradicts the ISA document or its own intent.
