docs.title: The engine in a system (sparc_apara)
docs.text:
From the hardware's Aa sources (cpu/ccu/ccu.aa, dma/control.aa, data_mem/*.aa), which the reference model does not cover:

# Source This model Why 26 dma/control.aa uses control-word bit 3 as interrupt enable, as the error flag on completion, and (written) to clear the interrupt; a command with it set never starts flags [0] scheduled, [1] started, [2] completed, [3] interrupt enable, [4] error one meaning per bit 27 CCU.TXT calls command 7 "wait-on-complete"; ccu.aa polls (non-blocking), so its interrupt fires only if a poll finds the thread already stopped without interrupt enable, a poll; with it, the command waits for the stop, then interrupts an interrupt a program can wait for 28 command 8 (step) executes the instruction in R2 at PC R1 one bundle from IMEM at R1, with local data only; R7 := the next PC debugging use 29 command 9 returns the RAS's 52-bit internal state R6 := depth, R7 := top 30 (reset leaves registers to the hardware's reset) reset keeps the registers, clears PC, RAS and ERROR registers set before a run survive a reset

Which addresses are local also follows the hardware: in a system, only the engine's own DMEM window is local, and every other address goes out to the system. The reference model aliases every address into DMEM, and the standalone apara configuration keeps that behavior.

The system's physical addresses (see The Engine in a System) follow the AJIT_APARA layout, with the addresses APARA's parameter template gives engine 0 of cluster 0.

docs.title: Cross-checking against the reference simulator
docs.text: validation/apara/run_tests.py --reference --mcode-run <path to mcode_run> also cross-checks the model against the reference simulator. For every test without a DEVIATION line, the model writes its final state (the PC, every register, and every DMEM word that is or was non-zero) as a results file, and the reference simulator, given the same program and inputs, must reach exactly that state. This checks the model and the test's own expectations at the same time.

docs.title: Open questions in the sources
docs.text:
Where the sources disagree or are silent, the model makes an explicit choice, listed here. D1 to D7 come from the first review of the sources, the rest from the findings since.

  • D1, opcode numbering from 0x16. The Aa_model's parameters.aa and OperatorClassification.txt disagree. The model uses the assembler's numbering (isa/parameters.aa) and keys its latencies by instruction class, not opcode.
  • D2, memory operations per bundle. The microarch doc says at most two (one per DMEM port); the slot rules, mcode_align and the reference documentation allow four. The model allows four, two ports, same-bank accesses one after another.
  • D3, slot rules. The model enforces the microarch doc's (and the assembler produces them).
  • D4, EXEC's structure. "Holds one bundle until the slowest finishes" versus "internally pipelined, full rate". The model is pipelined, results in order; engine.exec.pipelined = false gives the other.
  • D5, latencies. DIV and FSQRT 10 cycles (verbal), VREDUCE 2 and CMOV 1 (assumed): not in OperatorClassification.txt.
  • D6, the parameter template. Its comments and values disagree on the DMEM and configuration base addresses; the model follows the values (they agree with the AFB demultiplexer's decode).
  • D7, a push into a full RAS. Halts the thread (microarch doc) versus "blocks the engine" (ISA text): the model halts the thread.
  • Same-bank order. The microarch doc serializes same-bank accesses in slot order; the Aa_model does not fix an order. The model uses slot order.
  • Exception code 4, "integer square root of a negative number", is in the hardware's exception table, but isa.txt says there is no integer square root. The model has none (the code is unused).
  • The BTB is shared by the four threads; two threads' branches that alias to one entry evict each other. Modeled as described.
  • REGFILE and WRITEBACK. The microarch doc's channel table shows lock releases going from WRITEBACK to REGFILE, its text (from the Aa_model) has REGFILE reading EXEC's results and forwarding them to the retire daemon. The model follows the text; with two tokens it is the version that sustains one bundle per cycle.

docs.title: Findings of the validation suites
docs.text: The validation suites (validation/apara/, validation/sparc_apara/) also turned up places where the engine's ISA and microarchitecture documents are contradictory, ambiguous, or describe a design property worth a decision: for example, whether $set inserts or replaces, the limits of $pack and $dot, the branch predictor training only on mispredicts, returns being predicted by the BTB alone, the throughput limit of two REGFILE tokens, and the lack of an atomic read-modify-write. They are listed, each with the test that shows it, in docs/compliance/apara_specification_findings.md.

docs.title: APARA Instruction Set
docs.text:
This page is the programmer's reference for the APARA engine, as this project models it: what state a program sees, the data types its instructions work on, how instructions are grouped into bundles, and every instruction, with its assembly syntax and its encoding.

Where this description departs from the engine's own documents, the choice is listed in Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
An engine runs up to four hardware threads. They share the engine's memories and its pipeline, but each thread has its own architectural state:

State Size Notes PC 32 bits The address of the thread's next bundle, as an instruction-word index into IMEM, not a byte address. $r0 .. $r31 64 bits each General-purpose registers. $r0 always reads as 0, and writes to it are dropped. Return-address stack (RAS) 64 entries Return addresses: $call pushes one, $return pops one. ERROR 32 bits Why the thread stopped, see below.

Four threads let the engine stay busy: while one thread waits (for a result, a memory access, or a mispredicted branch), the pipeline runs the others.

docs.title: Memories
docs.text:
Memory Size Organization IMEM 16 KB, 4096 instruction words The program, shared by all four threads. The pipeline reads it 8 words (one line) at a time. DMEM 64 KB, 8192 64-bit words The data, shared by all four threads. Two banks of 32 KB (address bit 15 selects the bank), each accessed through its own port. Big-endian.

DMEM addresses are byte addresses. Each 64-bit word ("dword") is stored big-endian: the byte at an address with (address & 7) == 0 is the dword's most significant byte, bits [63:56].

What an address outside DMEM means depends on where the engine is:

  • On its own (the apara configuration), every data address aliases into DMEM, modulo 64 KB.
  • In a system (the sparc_apara configuration), DMEM appears at a window in the system's physical address space, and only addresses in that window are local. Every other address goes out to the system's memory, see The Engine in a System.

docs.title: How a thread runs and stops
docs.text:
A thread is inactive until it is started at some PC. It is then running, until it either executes $halt or meets an exception. Either way it is then halted, and its ERROR register says why:

ERROR bits Meaning 26 Return-address stack error: a $call with the RAS full, or a $return with it empty. 25 The thread executed $halt. 24 An exception stopped the thread. [23:0] One 3-bit exception code per bundle slot: slot s's code is in bits [3s+2 : 3s].

The exception codes:

Code Exception 1 Integer divide by zero. 2 Float divide by zero. 3 A float arithmetic result is not a number (NaN). 4 Reserved. The hardware's table lists "integer square root of a negative number", but there is no integer square root instruction. 5 Float square root of a negative number. 6 A memory address that is not a multiple of the transfer size. 7 An illegal instruction, an instruction in a slot it may not use (see Bundles), or no valid bundle at the PC (reported in slot 0).

A bundle that raises an exception changes nothing: no register, memory, or PC update happens, and the thread halts with its PC at that bundle. This makes the stopped state easy to examine: the PC names the bundle that failed, and the registers are as they were before it.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
Every instruction that operates on data names a type, written in parentheses: ($i32), ($vf16). A type gives an element width, and whether the elements are integers or floats, signed or unsigned, and one per register (a scalar) or packed several to a register (a vector).

Types Meaning $i4 $i8 $i16 $i32 $i64 Signed integers. $u4 $u8 $u16 $u32 $u64 Unsigned integers. $u128 $u256 2 and 4 registers, for memory transfers only. $f4 $f8 $f16 $f32 $f64 Floats. $vi4 .. $vi32, $vu4 .. $vu32, $vf4 .. $vf32 Vectors of signed, unsigned, or float elements.

docs.title: Scalars
docs.text: A scalar narrower than 64 bits lives in the low bits of a register. A signed operation sign-extends its operands from the type's width, and an unsigned integer operation uses the full 64-bit register values. Integer ALU results are always 64 bits. Float results are in the type's own format, in the register's low bits.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: A vector packs 64 / width elements into one register, with element 0 in the most significant bits. For example, $r1 = 0x0102030405060708, read as ($vi8), holds the eight elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, in that order. A vector operation works on every element at once, which is where the engine's speed on small data types comes from: one ($vi8) add is eight additions.

docs.title: Floats
docs.text:
f32 and f64 are IEEE single and double precision. The narrow formats are for low-precision work:

  • f16 is IEEE half precision (5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits, bias 15).
  • f8 has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits (bias 7).
  • f4 holds just the values ±{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, ∞, NaN}.

Arithmetic on the narrow formats is done in double precision and rounded back to the narrow format with one round bit (round half up on the magnitude), saturating to infinity, and flushing to zero below the smallest subnormal.

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
The engine is a VLIW (very long instruction word) machine: instead of discovering parallelism in hardware, it executes bundles of instructions that the program has already grouped to run together. A bundle holds 1, 2, 4, or 8 instructions of 32 bits each, all executed in the same step:

  • Every instruction of a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle. So a bundle that copies $r1 into $r2 and $r2 into $r1 swaps them.
  • Memory accesses happen in slot order: a load sees a store of an earlier slot of the same bundle.
  • No two instructions of a bundle may write the same register (the assembler checks this).

docs.title: Sizes and slots
docs.text:
A bundle's size, and which slot each instruction may occupy, follow the hardware's execution lanes:

  • A bundle that holds a branch, call, return, load, store, divide, or square root must have 8 slots. Any other bundle has the smallest power of two (1, 2, 4, or 8) that fits its instructions. Unused slots hold $null.
  • A bundle's address is a multiple of its size.
  • In an 8-slot bundle, a branch, call, or return must be in slot 0, a divide or square root in slot 1 (the engine has one shared divider), and loads and stores in slots 4 to 7 (the memory lanes).

You don't have to arrange any of this by hand. The assembler closes, pads, places, and arranges every bundle (see What the assembler does), and the engine checks the rules when it runs the bundle (exception 7 if one is broken).

In the encoded program, bit 31 of an instruction word is set on the first instruction of each bundle, which is how the engine finds bundle boundaries. Bits [30:26] are the opcode.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: The instructions below are shown in the syntax the assembler accepts. $rd is the destination register, $rs1 and $rs2 the sources, and imm a signed 10-bit immediate (-512 to 511).

docs.title: Arithmetic and logic (scalar)
docs.text:
+  $rd (type) $rs1 $rs2       // also: - * / | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ << >>
+  $rd (type) $rs1 imm

$rd = $rs1 op $rs2 (or $rs1 op imm). ~|, ~&, and ~^ are NOR, NAND, and XNOR.

  • Integer types have every operation. A signed >> is an arithmetic shift, shift counts use their low 6 bits, and / truncates toward zero. Dividing by zero raises exception 1.
  • Float types have only + - * /. Dividing by zero raises exception 2, and a NaN result exception 3.

docs.title: Vector arithmetic
docs.text:
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // also: - *
$v + $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2 $replicate     // $rs2's low element, used for every element

Element by element: element i of $rd is element i of $rs1 plus element i of $rs2. Integer results wrap around at the element width. With $replicate, every element of $rs1 is combined with the same value, $rs2's lowest element, for example to scale a vector.

docs.title: Dot product and reduction
docs.text:
$dot $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2                // the sum of the element products
$dot $accumulate $rd (vtype) $rs1 $rs2    // the same, plus $rd
$vreduce + $rd (vtype) $rs1               // also: * | & ^ ~^

$dot multiplies two vectors element by element and adds up the products. $vreduce combines all the elements of one vector with one operation. Integer dot products and reductions give a 64-bit result. Float ones give an f32, accumulated in single precision, one element at a time.

docs.title: Square root
docs.text:
$fsqrt $rd ($f32) $rs1                    // or ($f64)

A negative operand raises exception 5.

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
$cast (dtype) $rd (stype) $rs2

Converts $rs2, of type stype, to type dtype. Both types are scalars, or both are vectors.

  • A scalar cast converts the low bits of $rs2. Between integers, the value is sign- or zero-extended by the source type, then truncated to the destination width. Between integers and floats, the value is converted. A float-to-integer conversion truncates toward zero and saturates, and a NaN gives 0.
  • A vector cast converts every element, and may change the element width by one step at most ($vi8 to $vi16, for example, but not to $vi32). Widening doubles the data, so it writes two registers, $rd and $rd+1. Narrowing reads two, $rs2 and $rs2+1.

docs.title: Moving and arranging bits
docs.text:
$set   $rd index value          // $rd = value << (8*index); value 16 bits, index 0 to 7
$slice $rd high low $rs2        // $rd = bits [high:low] of $rs2
$pack  P $rd W $rs2             // the low W bits of $rs2, $rs2+1, ... packed into P bits
$cmov  (type) $rs1 cond [incr] $rd $rs2   // if $rs2 cond 0, then $rd = $rs1
  • $set loads a constant. value may be decimal, or hexadecimal written _h1234.
  • $pack gathers fields from consecutive registers: $pack 64 $r8 16 $r2 builds $r8 from the low 16 bits of $r2, $r3, $r4, and $r5, with $r2's field in the most significant position. A P larger than 64 writes P/64 registers.
  • $cmov is a conditional move. It tests its last register, $rs2, against 0. An optional increment (++1, --1, --2) is added to $rs2 after the test, which makes $cmov useful as a loop step too.

The conditions, for $cmov and for branches, compare a value with 0: == > < >= <= !=. Signed integers compare as values of the type's width, unsigned integers as 64-bit unsigned values, and floats by value (a NaN satisfies only !=).

docs.title: Loads and stores
docs.text:
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2]        $st (type) [$rs1 + $rs2] $rd
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + $rs2 ++n]    // then $rs2 += n * the transfer size (n: -16 to 15)
$ld (type) $rd [$rs1 + imm]

The address is $rs1 + $rs2 (or $rs1 + imm), and must be a multiple of the transfer size (exception 6 otherwise). The ++n form also steps $rs2 on, for walking through an array.

  • 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-byte transfers move one register. Signed loads sign-extend.
  • $u128 and $u256 move 2 and 4 registers, from $rd upward.
  • A vector type moves one element.

docs.title: Control transfer
docs.text:
? (type) $rs2 cond [incr] $goto label   // branch if $rs2 cond 0; then $rs2 += incr
$call label                             // or $call $rs2: the target is this address + $rs2
$return
$halt
$null

Branch and call targets are relative to the instruction's own address. $call pushes the address of the next bundle onto the RAS, and $return pops it. A branch's optional increment is -2 to 1, and is not allowed with a float test type. Like $cmov's, it lets one instruction both count a loop down and test it.

$halt stops the thread. $null does nothing, and fills the unused slots of a bundle.

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
The field layouts, as the assembler writes them. In every instruction word, bit 31 is the bundle start bit and bits [30:26] the opcode.

Instruction Opcode Fields ALU 0x04-0x0F type[25:21] rd[20:16] rs1[15:11] imm-flag[10] rs2[4:0] or imm10[9:0] VALU (ALU) as ALU, with a vector type, and replicate[10] FSQRT 0x10 type rd rs1 DOT 0x11 type rd rs1 accumulate[10] rs2 CAST 0x12 dest type[25:21] rd source type[14:10] rs2 LOAD, STORE 0x13, 0x14 type rd rs1 imm-flag[10] incr[9:5] rs2, or imm10[9:0] SET 0x15 byte index[23:21] rd value[15:0] VREDUCE 0x16 type rd rs1 operation[10:6] (an ALU opcode) CMOV 0x17 type rd rs1 cond[10:8] incr[7:6] rs2 PACK 0x18 rd log2(P)[15:12] log2(W)[11:9] rs2 SLICE 0x19 high[5:1] in [25:21], rd, high[0] in [15], low[14:9], rs2 BRANCH 0x02 type[25:22] cond[21:19] incr[18:17] offset12[16:5] rs2 CALL 0x01 label-flag[25], offset25[24:0] or rs2 RETURN, NULL, HALT 0x03, 0x1A, 0x1B

ALU opcodes: + 0x04, - 0x05, * 0x06, / 0x07, | 0x08, & 0x09, ^ 0x0A, ~| 0x0B, ~& 0x0C, ~^ 0x0D, << 0x0E, >> 0x0F.

Type codes: $i4..$i64 0x00-0x04, $u4..$u64 0x05-0x09, $f4..$f64 0x0A-0x0E, $u128 0x0F, $u256 0x10, $vu4..$vu32 0x11-0x14, $vf4..$vf32 0x15-0x18, $vi4..$vi32 0x19-0x1C.

docs.title: Writing and Running APARA Programs
docs.text:
The apara configuration is one APARA engine on its own, with no SPARC core around it. It is the place to write, run, and debug engine programs, and to study the engine's timing, before using the engine from a SPARC program (see The Engine in a System).

A run works like this: the simulator places the program in the engine's IMEM, the initial data in its DMEM, and the initial register values in its registers, starts one or more threads, and runs until every thread it started has stopped. It then reports how each thread stopped, and, if given the expected final state, checks it.

Like every configuration, apara comes as a fast functional model (cpp_model) and a cycle-level timing model (sitar_model), with the same command line.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
From the repo root:

model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/build.sh      # executable/apara_sim_cpp
model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/build.sh    # executable/apara_sim_sitar (needs the sitar CLI)

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
Assemble the program (see APARA Assembly Language and Tools), then run the object file:

python3 compiler/apara/apara_as.py prog.mcode
model/system_models/apara/cpp_model/executable/apara_sim_cpp \
        -p 0x0 -i prog.obj -d data.map -a registers.txt -r results.txt

The options:

Option Meaning -p <pc> Start a thread at <pc> (hexadecimal, an IMEM word index). Repeat it to start threads 1, 2, and 3 too. Without -p, one thread starts at 0. -i <file> The object file. -d <file> DMEM's initial contents (a data file). -a <file> Initial register values. -r <file> The expected final state. The run prints PASS, or the mismatches and FAIL. --dump-results <file> Write the final state as a results file (- for the screen). --stats Print statistics: per-thread counts (cpp_model), or the pipeline's counters (sitar_model, see APARA Timing Model). --trace Print every bundle executed (cpp_model). --max-bundles <n> / --max-cycles <n> Stop a run that does not end on its own (cpp_model / sitar_model). --latency-file <file> Change instruction latencies (sitar_model, see APARA Timing Model).

The file formats are described in File formats.

The exit status is 0 for PASS, or, without -r, when every thread stopped with $halt. It is 1 otherwise (a mismatch, an exception, or a thread still running at the limit), and 2 for an error in the command line or the files. That makes the simulators easy to use from scripts.

docs.title: Watching a program run
docs.text:
--trace prints one line per bundle executed: its thread and address, its instructions (without the $nulls), and, if it did not continue to the next bundle, where it went. For example, the end of a loop, from validation/apara/isa/control/control.mcode:

t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;  -> 0x0
t0 0x0:  ? ($i64) $r1 > --1 $goto pc+0;  + $r2 ($i64) $r2 $r1;
t0 0x8:  ? ($f32) $r3 < $goto pc+16;  -> 0x18
t0 0x18:  ? ($i16) $r4 < $goto pc+16;  + $r5 ($i64) $r0 1;  -> 0x28
t0 0x28:  $call pc+32;  + $r10 ($i64) $r0 16;  -> 0x48

The bundle at 0x0 branches back to itself while $r1 is above 0, counting $r1 down each time. On its last pass the branch is not taken, and the thread falls through to 0x8.

A thread that stops on an exception is reported with the slot and the cause:

thread 1: stopped at 0x8 by an exception: slot 4 unaligned memory address;

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
validation/apara/ holds the engine's own test suites, one folder each:

Folder Tests What they check isa/ 29 Every instruction, in one subfolder per class (alu_int, alu_float, vector, cast, bits, cmov, memory, control): each operation on each type, edge values (wraparound, sign extension, rounding), immediates and increments at their limits, and every exception. sequences/ 7 Instructions working together: full 8-slot bundles, loops, a recurrence in one bundle per step, a block copy with auto-increments, threads sharing DMEM, one thread's fault not stopping the others. hazards/ 10 The pipeline's handling of dependences between bundles (see Hazards). predictor/ 6 The branch predictor: loops, nested loops, two branches sharing a predictor entry, calls and returns. Each test's mispredict count is derived from the predictor's rules. asm_errors/ 21 Programs the assembler must reject: a register written twice in a bundle (also through multi-register writes and increments), too many control transfers, divides or memory operations in a bundle, values out of range, invalid types. timing/ 10 Microbenchmarks with exact cycle counts, derived by hand from the timing rules. Its README.md also has each test's counts for other settings of the knobs. kernels/ 6 Larger hand-scheduled programs: dot product, vector addition, SAXPY, reduction, and matrix products on one and four threads. c_programs/ 11 Programs compiled from C with the C compiler: the language's features, sorting, a prime sieve, and linear algebra. deviations/ 8 Behavior where the model departs, on purpose, from the engine's reference model (see Deviations and Findings).

Each folder has a README.md describing its tests.

docs.title: A test
docs.text:
A test is a source file and a .vprj file of the same name, in the same spirit as the SPARC tests (see Validation Suite). The .vprj says how to run the program and what to expect. For example, the timing test timing/t3_latency:

// Timing: EXEC latency. An f32 add takes 3 cycles in EXEC (cycles 3-5).
// The $halt behind it enters EXEC in cycle 4 but results leave in order,
// one per cycle: the add's in cycle 5, the halt's in 6; WRITEBACK in 8:
// 9 cycles.
//
    || + $r1 ($f32) $r2 $r3 ;
    || $halt ;

SOURCES = t3_latency.mcode
CYCLES = 9

RESULTS =

The source's header explains where the expected count comes from. A functional test sets registers and memory in INIT, and lists the expected results in RESULTS. From isa/control/control.vprj:

SOURCES = control.mcode

INIT =
r1 = 5
r3 = 0xbfc00000

RESULTS =
r1 = 0xffffffffffffffff
r2 = 0xf

The lines of INIT and RESULTS:

Line Meaning r3 = 0x10 Thread 0's $r3. t1.r3 = 0x10 Thread 1's $r3. m[0x80] = 0x0102030405060708 The DMEM dword (8 bytes) at byte address 0x80. m[C+0x8] = 0x2f2 In a C test: a dword of the global C. t1.pc = 0x9 (RESULTS only) Where thread 1 stopped. error = 0x2000000 (RESULTS only) Thread 0's ERROR register: 0x2000000 is a $halt.

A value in RESULTS may be followed by a mask, which selects the bits compared.

The other keys:

Key Meaning SOURCES = prog.mcode The program: mcode, C (.c, compiled first), or an object file (.obj). THREADS = 0x0 worker Start a thread at each of these IMEM addresses or labels. Default: one thread at 0x0. CYCLES = 12 The exact cycle count on the timing model, with the default timing settings. MISPREDICTS = 2, BTB_PREDICTIONS = 3 The exact branch predictor counts on the timing model. HAZARDS_UNLOCKED = 1 The hazards the timing model must count when built without the interlock (see Hazards). ASM_ERROR = written twice The program must not assemble, and the error message must contain this text. DEVIATION = <why> The test depends on one of the model's deviations. MAX_CYCLES = 100000 A larger limit, for a long test. APCC_FLAGS = -O0 Options for the C compiler.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py                          # every suite, on the cpp_model
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py --sitar                  # on the sitar_model, also checking the timing keys
python3 validation/apara/run_tests.py validation/apara/hazards --sitar   # one suite (or one .vprj)

The runner compiles or assembles each test, writes its files into validation/apara/build/<test>/, runs it, and prints PASS or FAIL for each, then a summary per suite:

PASS  timing/t1_halt.vprj
...
  asm_errors     21/21 passed
  c_programs     11/11 passed
...
  timing         10/10 passed
OVERALL: 108 passed, 0 failed

The apara configuration runs only these suites: the SPARC suites need a SPARC core (see Validation Suite).

docs.title: Adding a test
docs.text: Write a source file and its .vprj in a suite's folder, and run the suite. There is nothing to register: the runner finds every .vprj file in the folders it is given. To find the expected values of a new test, run it once with --dump-results - (see Running a program), and check every value by hand, or with an independent calculation, before writing it down.

docs.title: Hazards
docs.text:
A hazard is a bundle reading a register before an older bundle of the same thread has written its new value. The engine's pipeline resolves every such read-after-write dependence in hardware: DECODE tells REGFILE which registers a bundle reads and writes, and REGFILE holds a bundle until every register it reads or writes has been written back by the older bundles (see Register locks and tokens). A program, or a compiler, never needs to insert waits.

The other orderings are safe too:

  • Write after write: the same locks hold a bundle that writes a register an older bundle has yet to write, so the newer value always lands last.
  • Write after read: a bundle reads its registers when it is issued, in order, so a later bundle's write can never reach it.
  • Memory: a thread's loads and stores reach DMEM in program order.
  • Other threads: each thread has its own registers.

What the hardware does not resolve is within a single bundle: two instructions writing the same register (directly, or through a multi-register load, a cast's second register, or an increment). Every instruction of a bundle reads the registers as they were before the bundle, so a value written in a bundle cannot be read in the same bundle. The assembler rejects a register written twice (the asm_errors/ tests).

The timing model checks the interlock on every run, in two ways, and --stats reports both:

  • The lock masks. The registers each bundle actually reads and writes when it executes must be among those DECODE locked for it. Otherwise the model prints an internal error, since the interlock would have missed a dependence, and counts a lock-mask violation (lock-mask violations 0 otherwise). The test runner fails a test with any.
  • A hazard count, kept apart from the locks: a bundle issued while a register it reads still has an older write outstanding. With the interlock it must be 0 (RAW hazards 0).

The hazards/ tests check that the interlock is needed where it acts. Built with the knob engine.regfile.interlock = false (in model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/src/Top.sitar, see Knobs), REGFILE ignores its locks, and each hazards/ test must report exactly its HAZARDS_UNLOCKED count: the reads that would get a stale value without the interlock. The tests of independent bundles, write-after-write, and memory order must report none. Run them that way with --sitar: the runner then checks only the hazard counts, since the timing is no longer the engine's. Set the knob back to true, and rebuild, afterwards.

docs.title: The APARA Engine in a System (sparc_apara)
docs.text:
The sparc_apara configuration puts one APARA engine next to the SPARC core of core_l1cache_mmu_devices (with its L1 caches, MMU, and peripheral devices). A SPARC program uses the engine as an accelerator:

  1. It loads the engine's program into the engine's instruction memory (IMEM).
  2. It moves the input data into the engine's data memory (DMEM), either by writing it directly or by asking the engine's DMA unit to copy it from main memory.
  3. It starts one or more engine threads, and sets their registers first if they need arguments.
  4. It learns when the threads have stopped, by polling or by an interrupt, and how (a $halt, or an exception).
  5. It moves the results back, the same two ways.

All of this goes through memory-mapped registers: the engine's control unit (CCU), which carries out commands for each thread, and its DMA unit, which copies data between main memory and DMEM. The engine can also read and write main memory itself, with its ordinary loads and stores.

This page describes the system's parts and how they are connected, then the SPARC program's side: an example, the setup protocol step by step, the C routines, and the address map and registers they use. It ends with how the two models implement it, and the tests.

docs.title: How the parts are connected
docs.text:
The SPARC core reaches main memory, the devices and the engine through the system bus. The engine is the bus's second master: its DMA unit, and its own loads and stores outside DMEM, reach main memory through it too.

The SPARC and the engine communicate in four ways:

  • Commands, from the SPARC: writes to the control unit's registers load IMEM, set a thread's registers, start, reset or query a thread (see The control unit). Writes to the DMA unit's registers start copies (see The DMA unit).
  • Data in DMEM, which the SPARC reads and writes directly, through its window in the system's address space, or has the DMA unit copy.
  • Data in main memory, which the engine's own loads and stores, and its DMA unit, reach over the bus as its second master.
  • Completion, from the engine: a thread that stops (with $halt, or an exception) leaves a completion word for the SPARC to poll, and the control unit can raise an interrupt, which reaches the SPARC as IRL 14 through the Interrupt Controller. A DMA channel that finishes can do the same.

The engine's threads share its IMEM, DMEM and pipeline. Each has its own 32 registers, PC, return-address stack, and ERROR register.

In the timing model, these parts are modules joined by nets (see The models):

docs.title: An offload, step by step
docs.text:
The test validation/sparc_apara/basic/dma_dot_product/ offloads a dot product of two 32-element int8_t vectors to the engine. The engine's program, kernel.mcode, loads both vectors from DMEM, computes four 8-element dot products in one bundle, adds them up, and stores the 64-bit result back in DMEM:

// The dot product of two 32-element $i8 vectors in DMEM (at $r9 and
// $r10), stored as a 64-bit word at $r9 + 504. ($r9: DMEM's window
// address.)
start:
    ||
        $ld ($i64) $r1 [$r9 + 0]   $ld ($i64) $r2 [$r9 + 8]
        $ld ($i64) $r3 [$r9 + 16]  $ld ($i64) $r4 [$r9 + 24]
    ;
    ||
        $ld ($i64) $r5 [$r10 + 0]   $ld ($i64) $r6 [$r10 + 8]
        $ld ($i64) $r7 [$r10 + 16]  $ld ($i64) $r8 [$r10 + 24]
    ;
    ||
        $dot $r20 ($vi8) $r1 $r5   $dot $r21 ($vi8) $r2 $r6
        $dot $r22 ($vi8) $r3 $r7   $dot $r23 ($vi8) $r4 $r8
    ;
    || + $r24 ($i64) $r20 $r21   + $r25 ($i64) $r22 $r23 ;
    || + $r26 ($i64) $r24 $r25 ;
    || $st ($i64) [$r9 + 504] $r26 ;
    || $halt ;

The SPARC program's side, from dma_dot_product.c:

#include "kernel.mcode.h"   // kernel_program[], KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS, KERNEL_START

apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);             // 1. the program
apara_dma_start(0, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) a, 0, 1, 0, N, 0);      // 2. a -> DMEM 0
apara_dma_start(1, APARA_DMA_LOAD, (uint32_t) b, 256, 1, 0, N, 0);    //    b -> DMEM 256
apara_dma_wait(0);
apara_dma_wait(1);
apara_write_thread_register(0, 9, APARA_DMEM_BASE);                  // 3. arguments,
apara_write_thread_register(0, 10, APARA_DMEM_BASE + 256);
apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_START);                                  //    and start
apara_wait_thread(0);                                                 // 4. wait
apara_dma_store(2, (uint32_t) result, 504, 8);                       // 5. DMEM 504 -> result

Two DMA channels copy the two vectors at the same time. The engine's thread 0 gets the two vectors' DMEM addresses in $r9 and $r10, and runs from the label start. The SPARC program then waits for the thread to stop, and copies the result back to main memory with a third DMA channel.

docs.title: Setting up and running the engine
docs.text: This is the protocol a SPARC program follows to use the engine, with what is allowed at each step. Each step has a test in validation/sparc_apara/, named in brackets.

docs.title: At power-up
docs.text: No engine thread runs, and IMEM, DMEM and every register of every thread are zero (setup/cold_state). The engine's cycle counter runs from power-up. Nothing needs initializing before the first command.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Load the program into IMEM, a word at a time, through the control unit: apara_load_program(words, n). IMEM is shared by the four threads, so one program image serves all of them, and each thread starts at its own label. apara_read_imem reads a word back (setup/load_verify checks a whole image).

  2. Put the input data in DMEM, one of two ways:

    • directly, through the DMEM window, a 32-bit word at a time (apara_dmem_write_word). Simple, but each word is a bus access by the SPARC.
    • by DMA, which copies from main memory while the SPARC goes on with other work: apara_dma_load copies and waits, apara_dma_start and apara_dma_wait let the SPARC overlap several copies, or do its own work meanwhile. A copy can also gather strided data.

    An engine program compiled from C may also need its initialized globals: apara_load_dmem_image (see Carrying the engine's program). 3. Set each thread's registers, its arguments (apara_write_thread_register), and start it at an IMEM address (apara_start_thread). Threads may be started one after another, or at different times (threads/staggered). 4. Learn that the thread has stopped, by polling or by an interrupt (see below). The completion word says how: APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT for a thread that ended with $halt. After an exception it has APARA_ERROR_EXCEPTION and each slot's exception code (APARA_ERROR_CODE(word, slot)), and apara_thread_stop_pc gives the bundle that failed. 5. Collect the results from DMEM, directly (apara_dmem_read_word, apara_dmem_read_dword) or by DMA (apara_dma_store, to main memory). 6. Start again, for the next piece of work: a thread that stopped with $halt can be started again at once, with new registers. A thread stopped by an exception must be reset first (apara_reset_thread), which clears its PC, return-address stack and ERROR, and keeps its registers (interference/fault_isolation). A new program may be loaded over the old one between runs (setup/reload_program).

setup/offload_poll and setup/offload_interrupt do all six steps for an engine program compiled from C.

docs.title: Polling or an interrupt
docs.text:
• Polling. apara_poll_thread(t) returns 0 while the thread runs, and its completion word once it has stopped. apara_wait_thread(t) polls until then. Each poll is a control-unit command, several bus accesses, so a SPARC that only waits is simplest this way.
  • An interrupt. apara_request_completion_interrupt(t) asks the control unit to raise the engine's interrupt when thread t stops. The SPARC goes on with its own work. Its handler reads the completion word (apara_thread_completion), and clears the interrupt (apara_clear_interrupt). See Interrupts for the set-up.

Either way, each stop is reported exactly once: after a poll has returned a thread's stop, the next poll returns 0 until the thread has been started and has stopped again (threads/staggered). A program that polls several threads can therefore poll them in any order, and never counts one stop twice.

docs.title: What may happen while threads run
docs.text:
• Each thread on its own data. Threads do not disturb one another as long as each writes only its own part of DMEM (interference/disjoint_regions). One thread's exception stops only that thread (interference/fault_isolation).
  • The SPARC and the DMA unit may read and write other parts of DMEM while threads run, and may watch a running thread's progress word (interference/host_while_running, interference/dma_while_running).
  • Not while running: loading IMEM, or writing a running thread's registers. The control unit carries such commands out, but when they take effect in the running thread is undefined. Wait for the thread to stop first, or stop it with apara_reset_thread.

docs.title: Threads sharing data
docs.text: The engine's instruction set has no atomic read-modify-write. Threads that update the same DMEM word with a load, an add and a store race: another thread's update can fall between one thread's load and its store, and is lost (interference/shared_counter, where four threads each add 1, 1000 times, to one word, and the word ends below 4000). Threads should therefore work on their own data, and leave the SPARC to combine their results, as linalg/dot_threads does with four partial dot products.

docs.title: The SPARC's data cache
docs.text: The engine's windows are never cached, and the routines reach them with MMU-bypass accesses. Main memory may be cached, though (in the pages the MMU marks cacheable), and the caches do not see the engine's writes. After the DMA unit, or an engine program, writes main memory, the SPARC reads that data straight from memory, with an MMU-bypass load (the tests' physical_word), or flushes its data cache first (see Model Components).

docs.title: Floating point on the SPARC side
docs.text: The SPARC's startup code (compiler/crt0.s) leaves the FPU off. A SPARC program that computes with floats, to check an engine's float results for example, turns it on first, by setting the PSR's EF bit (linalg/saxpy).

docs.title: The routines
docs.text:
compiler/include/apara_access_routines.h has C routines for all of the steps above, in the same style as the device routines of ajit_access_routines.h (see C Programs). Every routine uses MMU-bypass accesses, so it works whether or not the MMU is enabled, and never goes through the caches.

Routine Does apara_load_program(words, n) Write words 0 to n-1 of IMEM. apara_write_imem(i, w), apara_read_imem(i) One IMEM word. apara_write_thread_register(t, r, v), apara_read_thread_register(t, r) A thread's 64-bit register. apara_start_thread(t, pc) Start thread t at pc (a label's address, from the program's header). apara_reset_thread(t) Stop thread t, and clear its PC, return-address stack, and ERROR. Its registers are kept. apara_poll_thread(t) The thread's completion word: 0 while it is running, or valid plus its ERROR once it has stopped. Each stop is reported once. apara_wait_thread(t) Poll until the thread stops, and return its completion word. apara_thread_stop_pc(t) Where the thread stopped. apara_request_completion_interrupt(t), apara_thread_completion(t), apara_clear_interrupt(t) Learn of the stop by interrupt instead, see Interrupts. apara_dma_start(c, op, src, dst, bursts, gap, bytes_per_burst, irq) Start DMA channel c, see The DMA unit. apara_dma_done(c), apara_dma_wait(c) Whether channel c has finished, and waiting for it. apara_dma_load(c, dmem, src, n), apara_dma_store(c, dst, dmem, n) One contiguous copy of n bytes into or out of DMEM, waiting for it. apara_dma_clear_interrupt(c) Clear channel c's interrupt. apara_dmem_write_word(o, v), apara_dmem_read_word(o) A 32-bit word of DMEM, at byte offset o, directly. apara_dmem_read_dword(o) A 64-bit word of DMEM (the high half at the lower address). apara_load_dmem_image(pairs, n) Write a C engine program's initialized globals into DMEM (see below). apara_read_timer() The engine's cycle counter.

The completion word's bits have names: APARA_COMPLETION_VALID, APARA_ERROR_HALT, APARA_ERROR_EXCEPTION, APARA_ERROR_RAS, and APARA_ERROR_CODE(word, slot) for a slot's exception code. A thread that ended with $halt reports APARA_COMPLETION_VALID | APARA_ERROR_HALT.

docs.title: Carrying the engine's program
docs.text:
An engine program travels inside the SPARC program as a C array. compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py assembles it and writes a header:

python3 compiler/apara/apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.mcode       # writes kernel.mcode.h

static const uint32_t kernel_program[] = { ... };   // IMEM words 0, 1, ...
#define KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS 33
#define KERNEL_START 0x0                             // each label's address

The names come from the file name (--name chooses another).

An engine program written in C (see The C Compiler) is handled the same way: apara_obj_to_c.py kernel.c compiles it for the system, with DMEM at its window address, and writes kernel.c.h. That header also gives each global variable's DMEM byte offset, and the DMEM words its initializers set:

#define KERNEL_DMEM_DATA 0x0                              // each global's DMEM offset
static const uint32_t kernel_dmem_image[] = { ... };     // (offset, value) pairs
#define KERNEL_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS 6

The SPARC program then loads the program and the initial data, puts its input at the globals' offsets, and reads the results from them:

apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
apara_load_dmem_image(kernel_dmem_image, KERNEL_DMEM_IMAGE_WORDS);
apara_dma_load(0, KERNEL_DMEM_DATA, (uint32_t) data, sizeof(data));

An __entry function's parameters arrive in $r1, $r2, ..., set with apara_write_thread_register before the thread starts. The image holds only the non-zero words: DMEM keeps whatever an earlier program left, so globals that must start at zero are cleared by the SPARC program, unless this is the first program since power-up.

A test in the validation suite names its engine programs in its .vprj, with an MCODE = kernel.mcode (or kernel.c) line, and validation/build_hex.py writes the headers before compiling (see Validation Suite).

docs.title: Address map
docs.text:
The system's physical addresses:

Range What 0x0000_0000 .. Main memory (256 MB), except: 0x0100_0000 .. 0x0100_FFFF The engine's DMEM, 64 KB. 0xFFFE_0000 .. 0xFFFE_007F The engine's control unit (CCU) registers. 0xFFFE_2000 .. 0xFFFE_207F The engine's DMA registers. 0xFFFF_0000 .. 0xFFFF_FFFF The peripheral devices.

Only main memory is ever cached, the engine's windows never are. A SPARC program should reach them with MMU-bypass accesses (ASI 0x20), as the routines above do. A program's own code and data must stay clear of the DMEM window, which lies inside main memory's range.

docs.title: The engine's own view
docs.text:
Inside the engine, an address in its own DMEM window is local, and every other address goes off island, out to the system, as in the hardware. So in a system, an engine program addresses its DMEM by the window's address. Usually the SPARC program passes that address in a register, as dma_dot_product does in $r9:

// $r9 = 0x01000000 (set by the SPARC): DMEM byte 0x100 is $r9 + 256.
    || $st ($i64) [$r9 + 256] $r3 ;

An engine load or store to any other address reaches main memory (or a device) through the system bus, which takes much longer than a DMEM access. The standalone apara configuration instead aliases every address into DMEM.

docs.title: The control unit
docs.text:
The control unit has a block of 8 32-bit registers for each of the engine's four threads, at 0xFFFE_0000 + 32*thread + 4*register. Commands for a thread go through its block.

Register Contents R0 Control: [31:16] sequence number, [15:14] a thread number (for command 9), [11:8] the command, and the flags [4] run the command interpreter, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, [0] start. (Bits [7:5], "init done" and "cpu mode" in the hardware, are kept but have no effect in the model.) R1 PC R2 IMEM index, or register number R3 IMEM write data, or timer high R4 IMEM read data, or timer low R5 Completion: [31] valid, [26] RAS error, [25] halt, [24] exception, [23:0] exception codes R6 Register high, or stop PC, or RAS depth R7 Register low, or next PC, or RAS top

To give a command, the host writes its arguments into R1 to R7, then writes R0 with the command and the flags start and run the command interpreter. The unit sets started, carries the command out, writes its results into the registers, and sets completed. The host polls R0 for completed before reading the results or giving the next command.

Command Does 1 read IMEM R4 := IMEM[R2] 2 write IMEM IMEM[R2] := R3. IMEM is shared by the threads, so any thread's block will do. 3 reset Stop the thread: PC 0, RAS and ERROR cleared, registers kept. 4 run Start the thread at R1. 5 read register R6:R7 := register R2 (high:low) 6 write register register R2 := R6:R7 7 completion Once the thread has stopped: R5 := valid plus its ERROR, and R6 := its PC (each stop is reported once). Before that, R5 := 0. With interrupt enable set, the command instead waits for the stop, and then raises the engine interrupt. 8 step Run one bundle at R1, with local data only. R7 := the next PC. 9 RAS state R6 := depth, R7 := top of the RAS of the thread named in R0[15:14]. 10 timer R3:R4 := the engine's cycle count.

Writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears the interrupt.

docs.title: The DMA unit
docs.text:
The DMA unit copies data between main memory and DMEM, while the SPARC and the engine both go on working. It has four independent channels, each with 8 registers at 0xFFFE_2000 + 32*channel + 4*register:

Register Contents R0 Control: [31:24] operation (1 load: main memory to DMEM, 2 store: DMEM to main memory), [23:20] and [19:16] the top 4 bits of the 36-bit source and destination addresses, [15:8] sequence number, and the flags [4] error, [3] interrupt enable, [2] completed, [1] started, [0] scheduled. R1, R2 Source and destination base addresses. R3 Total bytes (for the record only). R4 Number of bursts. R5 Gap: the distance between bursts. R6 Bytes per burst. Once completed: the stop cycle. R7 The start cycle.

The host writes R1 to R6, then writes R0 with the operation and scheduled, which starts the channel. A copy is a number of bursts, so one command can also collect or spread out strided data:

  • A load gathers: burst i comes from source + i·gap, and lands at destination + i·(bytes per burst), so the bursts end up packed together in DMEM.
  • A store scatters, the reverse: packed in DMEM, spread out in main memory.

For one contiguous copy, use a single burst. The DMEM-side address may be a DMEM byte offset or a window address. When the copy is done, the channel sets completed, and raises the engine interrupt if interrupt enable was set. Writing R0 with interrupt enable clear clears it. An unknown operation completes at once, with error set.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
Both units can interrupt the SPARC when something finishes: the control unit when a thread stops (command 7 with interrupt enable), and the DMA unit when a channel completes. Either one drives the Interrupt Controller's external input, IRL 14 (EXTERNAL_IRL).

A program that takes interrupts links the interrupt startup code (a STARTUP = crt0_interrupts.s line in its .vprj), and registers a handler with the dispatch routines of compiler/include/ajit_mt_irc.h (see Taking interrupts). From validation/sparc_apara/basic/run_interrupt/:

void engine_handler(void)
{
    completion = apara_thread_completion(0);   // the stop, as apara_poll_thread() would report it
    apara_clear_interrupt(0);                  // clear the source
}

int main(void)
{
    ajit_initialize_interrupt_handlers_to_null();
    ajit_set_interrupt_handler(EXTERNAL_IRL, engine_handler);
    writeInterruptControlRegister(0, 0, (1u << EXTERNAL_IRL) | 1u);   // slot 0: enable, IRL 14

    apara_load_program(kernel_program, KERNEL_PROGRAM_WORDS);
    apara_start_thread(0, KERNEL_LOOP);
    apara_request_completion_interrupt(0);
    ...                                        // the SPARC goes on with its own work
}

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Both models carry out the same commands with the same C++ classes: AparaControlCore (the control unit), AparaDmaCore (the DMA unit), and the engine itself, AparaCore. They differ, as in every configuration, in timing.

  • cpp_model The bus routes the engine's three windows to the engine, and the engine's off-island accesses and DMA transfers go back through the same bus. After every SPARC instruction, the engine runs one bundle, and the DMA unit moves one piece of a copy (up to 8 bytes).
  • sitar_model The engine's pipeline (AparaEngine, see APARA Timing Model) and its host side (AparaHost: the control and DMA units) are modules beside the core. The bus becomes an interconnect with two masters, the core and the host side, taken round robin. See Modules and nets below.

In the sitar_model, the parts divide the work like this:

Module Owns, does engine.exec The engine's state. Serves the host side's requests (DMEM, registers, IMEM, thread commands), one per cycle. Sends a bundle's off-island loads and stores to the host side, and holds the bundle until they are answered. Tells the host side when a thread stops. host The control unit's and DMA unit's registers and commands. Answers the SPARC's accesses to the engine's three windows, and sends DMA transfers and off-island accesses onto the bus. interconnect One transaction at a time, from the core or from the host side, to main memory, the devices, or the host side.

Every net crossing takes a cycle, so a SPARC access to a control-unit register crosses four nets (core to interconnect to host, and back), and one to DMEM six, since it also goes on to engine.exec, which owns DMEM.

docs.title: Modules and nets
docs.text:
System is that of core_l1cache_mmu_devices, with engine (the same AparaEngine module as in the apara configuration, see APARA Timing Model) and host added, and its bridge replaced by the two-master interconnect. The interconnect routes the SPARC's accesses to the engine's three windows to host, and carries host's DMA transfers and off-island accesses as its second master.

host reaches the engine's state in exec over five more nets: one pair for its requests to the engine (read a register, write IMEM, start a thread, ...), one pair for the engine's loads and stores that leave it, and one for the notice that a thread has stopped. The engine's interrupt goes from host to the Interrupt Controller's external input, IRL 14.

Top
 |
 +-- System (module)
      |
      +-- core : Core (module)
      |    |
      |    +-- sparcThread : SparcThread (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- caches : L1Caches (procedure)
      |    |
      |    +-- mmu : Mmu (procedure)
      |
      +-- interconnect : SystemInterconnect<2> (module)
      |
      +-- mainMemory : PhysicalMainMemory (module)
      |
      +-- devices : PeripheralDevices (module)
      |
      +-- engine : AparaEngine (module: fetch, decode, regfile, exec, writeback, as in apara)
      |
      +-- host : AparaHost (module)

core.requestOut                   --coreRequestNet-->       interconnect.masterRequestIn[0]
core.responseIn                   <-coreResponseNet--       interconnect.masterResponseOut[0]
host.masterRequestOut             --hostRequestNet-->       interconnect.masterRequestIn[1]
host.masterResponseIn             <-hostResponseNet--       interconnect.masterResponseOut[1]
interconnect.memoryRequestOut     --memoryRequestNet-->     mainMemory.requestIn
interconnect.memoryResponseIn     <-memoryResponseNet--     mainMemory.responseOut
interconnect.devicesRequestOut    --devicesRequestNet-->    devices.requestIn
interconnect.devicesResponseIn    <-devicesResponseNet--    devices.responseOut
interconnect.engineRequestOut     --engineRequestNet-->     host.slaveRequestIn
interconnect.engineResponseIn     <-engineResponseNet--     host.slaveResponseOut
devices.interruptLevelOut         --interruptLevelNet-->    core.interruptLevelIn
host.interruptOut                 --engineInterruptNet-->   devices.externalInterruptIn
host.serviceOut                   --serviceRequestNet-->    engine.exec.serviceIn
host.serviceIn                    <-serviceResponseNet--    engine.exec.serviceOut
engine.exec.offIslandOut          --offIslandRequestNet-->  host.offIslandIn
engine.exec.offIslandIn           <-offIslandResponseNet--  host.offIslandOut
engine.exec.stopOut               --stopNet-->              host.stopIn

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
validation/sparc_apara/ holds the tests of the SPARC using the engine. Each is a bare-metal SPARC C program, with one or more engine programs, built and run like the other C tests (see Validation Suite), on --config sparc_apara. On the sitar_model, give them a larger cycle limit:

python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara --config sparc_apara
python3 validation/run_tests.py validation/sparc_apara --config sparc_apara --sitar --max-cycles 50000000

Every test reports like the device tests: %o0 = 1 if every check passed, and %o1 has one bit per check, listed in the test's header comment. The SPARC program computes the expected results itself.

Folder Tests What they check basic/ 8 Each part of the engine's interface on its own: IMEM and registers, running and polling, the completion interrupt, exceptions, four threads, the engine's own main-memory accesses, DMA and its interrupt, and a whole offload by DMA (dma_dot_product). setup/ 5 Bringing the engine up, one thread: its state at power-up, loading and reading back its memories, complete offloads of a program compiled from C (by polling and by interrupt), and loading a second program over the first. threads/ 5 The same program on 1, 2, 3 and 4 threads, each on its own slice of the data, and threads started and restarted at different times. interference/ 5 Whether threads, the SPARC and the DMA unit disturb one another (see What may happen while threads run), and the one real interference, a race on shared data. linalg/ 3 Linear algebra offloaded to the engine: an 8x8 matrix product on four threads, SAXPY in floating point, and a four-thread dot product compiled from C.

Each folder has a README.md describing its tests, and validation/sparc_apara/README.md summarizes the protocol above.

docs.title: APARA Timing Model
docs.text:
The sitar_model of the apara configuration is a cycle-level model of the engine's pipeline, following the APARA microarchitecture document, and is the same pipeline sparc_apara uses.

As everywhere in this project, the model keeps function and timing apart. What each bundle does comes from the same C++ class the fast functional model runs, so the two models always compute the same results. The timing comes from the Sitar structure itself: the pipeline's stages are modules, the channels between them are nets, and a bundle's time is spent actually waiting in them, for a free channel, a register, or the divider. It is never computed after the fact. This is what makes the timing model trustworthy for experiments: change a channel depth or a latency, and every effect it has on the rest of the pipeline follows by itself.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
The engine's five stages, each a module, are joined by nets with the hardware's channel depths: 2 entries, except 1 for EXEC's results and for WRITEBACK's notices to FETCH. Each module takes its inputs in the first half of a cycle and sends its outputs in the second half, so a bundle spends at least one cycle in each stage. A stage whose output channel is full holds its bundle until there is room, and the stages before it then fill up and wait too. This is the hardware's elastic pipeline.

  • FETCH Picks a running thread (round robin), reads the 8-word IMEM line holding its PC, and sends that line's bundles to DECODE, one per cycle and in PC order, before picking another thread. It predicts each bundle's next PC with the branch target buffer (BTB).
  • DECODE Decodes a bundle: which registers it reads and writes, how long it will take in EXEC, and whether it needs the divider. It then sends the bundle on to REGFILE, on its thread's own channel.
  • REGFILE Holds one waiting bundle per thread. Each cycle it issues one of them (round robin) whose registers are all free, provided a token is free, and locks the registers that bundle will write. When the bundle's result comes back from EXEC, it releases those locks and the token.
  • EXEC Executes the bundle, then holds it for its latency. EXEC owns the engine's state: its memories, registers, and threads. It skips bundles fetched on a wrong path.
  • WRITEBACK Retires the bundle. It sends FETCH a PC correction when a bundle's next PC was mispredicted, and a notice when a thread has stopped.

docs.title: A bundle's journey
docs.text: A bundle with no stalls is fetched in some cycle c, decoded in c+1, issued by REGFILE in c+2, and executed in EXEC from c+3. Its result comes back to REGFILE after its latency, and it leaves WRITEBACK one cycle later. So a program of one 1-cycle bundle takes 6 cycles from start to finish. Later bundles overlap with it, so a stream of independent bundles completes at one bundle per cycle.

docs.title: Modules and nets
docs.text:
The apara configuration's Top holds one AparaEngine and nothing else: there is no SPARC core and no system around it. This shows which design unit instantiates which, and the nets joining the stages.

Top
 |
 +-- engine : AparaEngine (module)
      |
      +-- fetch     : AparaFetch (module)
      |
      +-- decode    : AparaDecode (module)
      |
      +-- regfile   : AparaRegfile (module)
      |
      +-- exec      : AparaExec (module)
      |
      +-- writeback : AparaWriteback (module)

fetch.toDecode          --fetchToDecode-->          decode.fromFetch
decode.toRegfile[0..3]  --decodeToRegfile[0..3]-->  regfile.fromDecode[0..3]
regfile.toExec          --regfileToExec-->          exec.fromRegfile
exec.toRegfile          --execToRegfile-->          regfile.fromExec
regfile.toWriteback     --regfileToWriteback-->     writeback.fromRegfile
writeback.correctionOut --correctionNet-->          fetch.correctionIn
writeback.haltOut       --haltNet-->                fetch.haltIn
exec.fetchControlOut    --fetchControlNet-->        fetch.controlIn

decodeToRegfile is one net per thread, so REGFILE can hold a waiting bundle of each thread and issue whichever one is ready. fetchControlNet carries thread starts and resets to FETCH.

docs.title: Instruction latency
docs.text:
A bundle's time in EXEC is the latency of its slowest instruction, or the time of its memory accesses if that is longer. The latencies come from a table, by instruction class. The defaults:

Entry Cycles Covers nop any, control any, halt any, misc any, logic any 1 $null, branches/calls/returns, $halt, $set $slice $pack, | & ^ ~| ~& ~^ arith int<=32, arith fp<=16 1 + - *, scalar and vector arith int64 2 arith fp32, arith fp64 3 shift int<=32 / shift int64 1 / 2 << >> dot int<=32, dot fp<=16 / dot int64, dot fp32, dot fp64 2 / 3 cast narrow / cast wide 1 / 2 narrow: integer to integer, float to integer, floats up to f16 vreduce any 2 assumed: not in the hardware's table cmov any 1 assumed: not in the hardware's table memory local 3 a bundle's DMEM accesses divide any, sqrt any 10 the designer's figure, to be confirmed

To try other latencies, pass --latency-file <file> to the apara simulator. Each line of the file overrides one entry, as <class> <operands> <cycles>, and # starts a comment:

arith fp32 5     # an f32 add/subtract/multiply takes 5 cycles
divide any 20

docs.title: Data memory
docs.text: DMEM has two banks (address bit 15 selects the bank), each with its own 256-bit port. A bundle's accesses to different banks proceed in parallel. Accesses to the same bank go one after another, each extra one adding a cycle (the bankConflictCycles knob). Placing two arrays that are read together in different banks avoids the conflict.

docs.title: The divider
docs.text: Integer and float divides and square roots share one divider. A bundle that needs it waits in EXEC until the previous user has finished.

docs.title: EXEC
docs.text: By default EXEC is internally pipelined: it takes a new bundle every cycle, and results leave it in order, one per cycle. The pipelined knob selects instead a stage that holds one bundle for its whole latency.

docs.title: Register locks and tokens
docs.text:
A bundle waits in REGFILE while any register it reads or writes is locked by an earlier bundle of its thread, that is, until the earlier bundle's result is back. This is how the pipeline keeps a thread's bundles in order without stalling the other threads.

At most 2 bundles are in EXEC at a time, one per REGFILE token. A token comes back with the bundle's result, two cycles after issue for a 1-cycle bundle, so two tokens are exactly enough to issue one bundle every cycle.

docs.title: Branch prediction
docs.text:
The branch target buffer has 256 entries, direct mapped by the low 8 bits of a bundle's PC, and shared by the four threads. Each entry holds a 22-bit tag, a 2-bit counter (0 strongly taken, 3 strongly not taken), and a target. A lookup predicts the entry's target if the tag matches and the counter is below 3, and otherwise the next bundle.

Only PC corrections train the BTB: a correction to a taken branch lowers the counter and sets the target, one to a not-taken branch raises the counter, and a new entry starts at 0 or 3 accordingly.

Calls and returns are predicted the same way, by their BTB entry: a $return is predicted to go where it went last time. Some consequences for programs, each measured by a test in validation/apara/predictor/:

  • A loop's closing branch mispredicts once per run of the loop, at its exit, once the BTB has learned it.
  • A correctly predicted branch never trains its entry. So a loop that is entered again and again (an inner loop) pulls its counter up by one at each exit, and after three exits the entry predicts "not taken": from then on every run of the inner loop mispredicts twice, at its first pass and at its exit (nested_loops).
  • A function called from several places mispredicts its return whenever the caller changes (call_sites).
  • Two branches whose PCs share their low 8 bits share an entry, and evict each other (alias).

docs.title: Mispredicts
docs.text: EXEC compares each bundle's actual next PC with the one FETCH predicted. On a mismatch, the thread's following bundles, already fetched on the wrong path, are skipped (not executed, though their register locks are still released) until FETCH, corrected by WRITEBACK, sends the first bundle of the right path. With one thread, a mispredict costs 5 cycles. With several, the other threads keep the pipeline busy meanwhile. A thread's halting bundle is handled the same way, except that the thread then stays stopped.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text:
All the timing knobs are set in one place, Top.sitar in apara (model/system_models/apara/sitar_model/src/Top.sitar) and System.sitar in sparc_apara. Rebuild after a change.

Knob Default Meaning engine.fetch.imemDelay 0 Cycles between FETCH picking a thread and its IMEM line arriving. engine.exec.pipelined true false: EXEC holds one bundle for its whole latency. engine.exec.latency.bankConflictCycles 1 Cycles per extra same-bank access in a bundle. engine.regfile.tokens 2 How many bundles may be in EXEC at once. engine.regfile.interlock true false: REGFILE ignores its register locks, to show which reads would be hazards without them (see Hazards). Not a hardware option.

--stats prints the pipeline's counters: bundles fetched, executed, and skipped, mispredicts, fetches that followed a BTB prediction, the cycles lost to register locks, to tokens, and to the divider, bank conflicts, and the two hazard checks (see Performance Modeling).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The timing model is checked by three suites in validation/apara/, each count derived by hand from the rules above, and written in the test's header:

  • timing/, microbenchmarks with exact cycle counts: one bundle (6 cycles), a stream of bundles at full rate, latency, a read-after-write stall against the independent case, the shared divider, a bank conflict against the same accesses on two banks, a mispredict, and two threads sharing the pipeline.
  • predictor/, exact mispredict counts for loops, nested loops, aliasing entries, and calls and returns.
  • hazards/, the register interlock (see Hazards).

run_tests.py --sitar checks every count exactly. The counts are derived for the default knob values and latency table, so the suite checks the timing model at those settings only. Each knob was also checked by setting it to several values, one at a time: every count moved by exactly the amount the rules predict. timing/README.md has those counts, and how to set the knobs back to their defaults afterwards.

The kernels and C programs of the other suites run on the timing model too, and their --stats show where a larger program spends its cycles. For example, an 8x8 matrix product (kernels/matmul_i8) takes 122 cycles on one thread and 112 on four: its memory-heavy bundles stay in EXEC 3 cycles or more, so the two REGFILE tokens, not the threads, limit its throughput.

The open items, such as the latencies marked above, EXEC's structure, and the order of same-bank accesses, are listed in Deviations and Findings.

docs.title: log_viewer/
docs.text: A lightweight, self-contained, single-file browser tool for viewing SPARC V8 instruction/state traces produced by CoreLogger (model/cpp_common_code/CoreLogger.h) -- used by every configuration's cpp_model and sitar_model, since both drive the same SparcCore and therefore emit the same trace format.

docs.title: What's here
docs.text:
• viewer.html -- the viewer itself. A single HTML file, no build step, no external dependencies (works entirely offline, nothing is fetched from the network). Open it directly in any modern browser.
  • test_simple_ADD.log / test_simple_ADD.objdump -- symlinks to a small sample trace and its matching disassembly, generated from the bundled test_simple_ADD example (see below and ../validation/README.md), so you can explore the viewer without building or running anything first. Named to match, not sim_trace.*, so it's the same file the walkthroughs elsewhere produce, not a differently-named copy.

docs.title: Trace format
docs.text: Tab-separated, one row per architectural event (FETCH, TRAP_RAISED, TRAP_ENTER, MEM_READ, MEM_WRITE, ATOMIC, RESET, ANNUL, HALT, or a generic one-off): seq, time, pc, event, detail, followed by the entire current-window processor state (PSR fields named and in binary, general registers in hex). See CoreLogger.h for exactly what each event logs and why. The viewer only requires seq/time/pc/ event/detail to be present -- any extra columns a future trace source adds are simply ignored, not required.

docs.title: Viewing a trace
docs.text:
1. Build the cpp model with logging enabled, and run a test program: 
    model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
    This writes test_simple_ADD.log into the current directory (a trace file is always named after the hex file it ran).
  2. Open log_viewer/viewer.html in a browser (double-click it, or open log_viewer/viewer.html / xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html).
  3. Click Load trace and pick test_simple_ADD.log; click Load objdump and pick validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump (the matching disassembly, see ../validation/README.md).

docs.title: Example: viewing the bundled test_simple_ADD example
docs.text:
From the repository root:

model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/cpp_model/executable/sparc_sim_cpp_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex
open log_viewer/viewer.html   # or: xdg-open log_viewer/viewer.html

Then in the viewer: Load trace -> test_simple_ADD.log (written into the repository root, since that's where the command above was run from), Load objdump -> validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.objdump.

docs.title: The same, via the sitar model
docs.text:
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/build.sh --logging
model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/executable/sparc_sim_sitar_core_only_logging \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.hex \
    validation/test_simple_ADD/test_simple_ADD.expected

Writes test_simple_ADD.log (sparcThread's trace, directly loadable, same as above) and sitar.log (everything else Sitar logs -- see model/system_models/core_only/sitar_model/README.md) into the current directory.

docs.title: Optional: serve it for auto-loading
docs.text:
If you'd rather not click through file pickers every time, serve the directory containing both files and pass them as URL query parameters -- the viewer fetch()es them automatically on load:

cd log_viewer
python3 -m http.server 8000

then open http://localhost:8000/viewer.html?trace=test_simple_ADD.log (the bundled sample -- the viewer also automatically tries the same basename with a .objdump extension, test_simple_ADD.objdump here). For a freshly generated trace, copy it (and its .objdump) into this directory first, or point ?trace= at a relative path if your server root already covers both files. This only works over http(s), not a plain file:// URL -- browsers block a page from reading another local file just by name.

docs.title: Using the viewer
docs.text:
• Search: field=value (e.g. PC=0x1c, l4=0x3434, T=56) matches a specific column; plain text with no = searches every column for a substring.
  • prev / next: step through search matches only. Use the Up/Down arrow keys to step through the trace row by row regardless of search.
  • Click a row in the Trace panel to select it and see its state. Click a line in Disassembly to jump to the first trace row at that address.
  • The Trace panel's event column is colored by event type (e.g. FETCH amber, EXECUTED green, the two trap events orange, HALT red, RESET purple, memory events blue), so a given kind of row is easy to pick out while scanning.
  • All three panels (Disassembly, Trace, State) are independently resizable -- drag the thin dividers between them.
  • Light/dark theme toggle, top right.
